questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior triangle of the neck, include the following Except one:
questions.explanation: The occipital triangle is located in the posterior triangle of the neck, not the anterior triangle. The anterior triangle boundaries are: sternocleidomastoid (posterior), sternohyoid (anterior), and superior border of mandible (superior).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior triangle of neck is bounded by sternocleidomastoid, sternohyoid, and mandible; contains carotid, muscular, digastric, and submental triangles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The roots of the brachial plexus pass between:
questions.explanation: The roots of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) pass between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius muscles. This anatomical relationship is clinically important for thoracic outlet syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Brachial plexus roots emerge between anterior and middle scalene muscles before forming trunks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed by:
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed by both the thalamus (superior part) and hypothalamus (inferior part). The interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia) connects the two thalami.
questions.keyConcept: Third ventricle lateral wall = thalamus (dorsal) + hypothalamus (ventral).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sensations received by the thalamus are Except:
questions.explanation: The thalamus receives exteroceptive, proprioceptive, gustatory, visual, and auditory sensations but NOT smell (olfactory). Olfaction is the only special sense that does not relay through the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamus acts as sensory relay station for all senses except olfaction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nucleus Ventralis posterior of thalamus receives the following Except:
questions.explanation: The lateral lemniscus carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei to the inferior colliculus, bypassing the VPL nucleus. The VPL receives medial lemniscus, spinal lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus, and fibers from nucleus solitarius.
questions.keyConcept: VPL receives touch, proprioception, pain, temperature via medial/spinal/trigeminal lemniscus; auditory bypasses via lateral lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following are efferent hypothalamic fibers Except:
questions.explanation: Corticohypothalamic fibers are afferent (going TO hypothalamus FROM cortex), not efferent. Efferent hypothalamic tracts include supraoptic hypophyseal, tuberoinfundibular, mamillotegmental, and paraventriculohypophyseal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamic efferent tracts: supraoptic-hypophyseal, tuberoinfundibular, mamillotegmental, paraventriculohypophyseal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle) forms the anterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. The posterior boundary is the pontine tegmentum and the fossa floor is the posterior perforated substance.
questions.keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa boundaries: anterolateral = crus cerebri; posterior = tegmentum; floor = perforated substance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding Broca’s area, select the correct answer:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus (not middle) and is a motor speech center (not sensory). It is present in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) and is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not anterior cerebral artery.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area: motor speech center in inferior frontal gyrus of dominant hemisphere, supplied by MCA.
options: It is a sensory speech center
It is located in middle frontal gyrus
It is present in the dominant hemisphere
It is supplied by anterior cerebral artery
None of the above is correct

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Frontal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following functions Except:
questions.explanation: Understanding received auditory information (receptive language) is a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe handles speech production, skilled movements, eye movement initiation, and behavior control.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe functions: speech production (Broca), skilled movements, conjugate eye movements, behavior control.
options: Initiation of conjugate lateral eye movements

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Frontal lobe in the non-dominant hemisphere contains the following areas Except:
questions.explanation: Wernicke's speech area is located in the temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus), not in the frontal lobe of the non-dominant hemisphere. The non-dominant hemisphere contains the same motor areas as the dominant but lacks speech areas.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant hemisphere frontal lobe contains motor areas (4,6,8) but NOT Wernicke's area (temporal lobe).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the first visual area (17):
questions.explanation: All statements about visual area 17 are true: it lies on both banks of the calcarine sulcus, extends onto the occipital pole, is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, and lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
questions.keyConcept: Primary visual cortex (V1): straddles calcarine sulcus, supplied by PCA, lesions cause contralateral visual field defects.
options: Lies above and below the post calcarine sulcus
Is supplied by posterior cerebral artery
Its lesion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia
All of the above is true

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the motor speech center, all the statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not the anterior cerebral artery. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes. All other statements about motor speech center are true.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area supplied by MCA; damage causes expressive aphasia; connected to Wernicke's area.
options: Found in the inferior frontal gyrus
Its lesion leads to expressive aphasia
Is supplied by anterior cerebral artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Parietal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following Except:
questions.explanation: Facial recognition (prosopagnosia) is a function of the fusiform face area in the inferior temporal lobe, not the parietal lobe. The dominant parietal lobe handles stereognosis, cutaneous and proprioceptive perception, and language comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal lobe: stereognosis, sensation, proprioception; prosopagnosia involves temporal fusiform area.
options: Comprehension of received auditory & visual information

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle derived from the third pharyngeal arch:
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle is derived from the third pharyngeal arch. The stapedius, superior parathyroid, and cricothyroid derive from the second, fourth, and fourth arches respectively. The platysma derives from the second arch.
questions.keyConcept: Pharyngeal arch muscles: 1st = mastication; 2nd = facial expression; 3rd = stylopharyngeus; 4th = pharynx/larynx.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The hyoid bone is derived from:
questions.explanation: The hyoid bone develops from migrating paraxial mesoderm of the second and third pharyngeal arches. The greater horn and upper body come from 3rd arch; lesser horn and lower body from 2nd arch.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoid: body and greater horn from 3rd arch mesoderm; lesser horn from 2nd arch mesoderm.
options: Migrating neural crest cells of 1st & 2nd arches
Migrating neural crest cells of 2nd & 3rd arches

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The two bones that develop from the 1st pharyngeal arch are:
questions.explanation: The malleus and incus develop from the first pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch). The stapes develops from the second arch. This is why the stapedius muscle (2nd arch) is innervated by the facial nerve while tensor tympani (1st arch) is innervated by V3.
questions.keyConcept: First pharyngeal arch derivatives include malleus and incus (plus muscles of mastication, V2/V3 nerves).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning synapses:
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are widely distributed in the CNS, not rare. Electric synapses are characterized by rapid transmission without delay, are bidirectional (not unidirectional), and do not use gap junctions in the typical chemical synaptic cleft.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses: neurotransmitter-based, drug-sensitive, unidirectional, wide distribution in CNS.
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse
Chemical synapses are affected by many drugs & chemicals
In chemical synapses, gap junction conduct impulses between presynaptic & postsynaptic structure

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding neurotransmitters:
questions.explanation: Dopamine function is primarily related to movement and motivation, not mood (that is serotonin/norepinephrine). ACh is excitatory at NMJ but can be inhibitory centrally. Catecholamines are fast transmitters. Glutamate is excitatory; GABA is inhibitory.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine: basal ganglia pathway for movement. ACh: excitatory at NMJ. GABA: main inhibitory transmitter.
options: Dopamine function is related to mood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The mechanism of synaptic transmission includes:
questions.explanation: Ca++ ions enter the presynaptic terminal (not released from it) to trigger vesicle fusion. Presynaptic knobs release both excitatory and inhibitory transmitters. Transmitters cause either EPSPs or IPSPs. Excitatory transmitters cause depolarization (not hyperpolarization).
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic transmission: Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis; transmitter binds specific receptors causing EPSP or IPSP.
options: Ca++ ions are released from the presynaptic knob
Presynaptic knobs release only an excitatory transmitter
Chemical transmission causes development of only excitatory postsynaptic state
Excitatory transmitters hyperpolarize the postsynaptic membrane
The released transmitter combines with specific receptors on postsynaptic membrane

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding sensory receptors:
questions.explanation: According to Müller's law of specific nerve energies, each receptor is specific to its adequate stimulus. Receptors have LOW threshold for their specific stimulus. Receptor potential is directly proportional to stimulus intensity, not inversely.
questions.keyConcept: Law of specific nerve energies: each receptor responds only to its adequate stimulus at low threshold.
options: Receptors are non-specific to stimuli according to Muller’s law
Stimulation of certain receptors can produces different modalities of sensations
Receptors are stimulated by adequate stimuli at a low threshold
Receptor potential is inversely related to the intensity of stimulus according to Weber Fechner law
The same receptor may be stimulated by different stimuli to produce different sensations

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding Crude Touch sensation:
questions.explanation: Crude touch is one of the protopathic (primitive) sensations along with pain and temperature. It is transmitted through the anterior spinothalamic tract (not dorsal column), perceived at the level of the thalamus (not cortex), and uses free nerve endings (not Meissner's corpuscles).
questions.keyConcept: Protopathic sensations (crude touch, pain, temperature) travel via anterolateral system; epicritic (fine touch, vibration) via dorsal column.
options: Is perceived at the level of the sensory cortex
Is transmitted through dorsal column pathway
Is better felt in non-hairy skin areas
It is one of the protopathic sensations

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
In Thermal sensations, all of the following are true EXCEPT:

A) Cold receptors are more numerous than Hot receptors, but Hot receptors adapt more rapidly than cold receptors.
B) Are transmitted through lateral division of anterolateral system.
C) Temperature higher than 45°C produces hot pain and temperature lower than 10°C produces cold pain.
D) The maximal discharge of hot receptors occurs at 45°C and of cold receptors occurs at 25°C.
E) They are carried by Aβ fibers.
questions.explanation: Thermal sensations are carried by Aδ fibers (cold) and C fibers (hot), not Aβ fibers. Aβ fibers carry touch, pressure, and vibration. Cold receptors adapt slower than hot receptors, and maximal discharge occurs at 25°C (cold) and 45°C (hot).
questions.keyConcept: Temperature sensation: Aδ (cold, 10-40°C), C fibers (heat, 30-45°C); transmitted via spinothalamic tract.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Pain produced by tissue damage is due to release of:

A) Excess norepinephrine.
B) ATP.
C) Kinins.
D) Heparin.
E) Dopamine.
questions.explanation: Kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) are released during tissue damage and are potent pain-producing substances. They sensitize nociceptors. ATP also contributes but kinins are the primary algogenic substance among these options.
questions.keyConcept: Pain mediators: bradykinin, histamine, serotonin, ATP, prostaglandins - released from damaged tissue.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Substantia Gelatinosa of Rolandi can NOT be inhibited by:

A) Stimulation of Aβ fibres.
B) Release of endorphins from the hypothalamus.
C) Counter irritant.
D) Aquipuncture
E) Herpes Zoster.
questions.explanation: Herpes Zoster activates (rather than inhibits) substantia gelatinosa by causing nociceptive input. Aβ fiber stimulation, endorphins, counter-irritants, and acupuncture all inhibit SG via presynaptic inhibition or descending pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia Gelatinosa modulates pain via T-junction; inhibited by Aβ stimulation, endorphins, counter-irritants.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
A patient who has had destruction of somatic sensory area I on the left side will show:

A) Total lack of pain sensation on the same side:
B) Total lack of temperature sensation of the same side.
C) Inability to identify objects put in the left hand.
D) Astereognosis in the right hand.
questions.explanation: Destruction of the left somatic sensory area I causes astereognosis (inability to identify objects) in the RIGHT hand because sensory pathways cross. Total loss of sensation would require bilateral lesions. Wernicke's area (temporal) handles auditory comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral sensory cortex destruction causes astereognosis in opposite hand; object identification requires cortical processing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:

A) They are larger and more numerous than gamma neurons.
B) They supply extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.
C) Alpha in the lateral part of anterior horn is concerned with fine movements.
D) Alpha of flexors is dorsally present to alpha of extensors
E) All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit.
questions.explanation: Alpha motor neurons that supply a specific muscle do NOT represent one motor unit; a motor unit is one alpha motor neuron plus ALL the muscle fibers it innervates. Multiple alpha neurons contribute to each muscle. The statement is false because it contradicts the definition of motor unit.
questions.keyConcept: Motor unit = 1 α-motor neuron + all muscle fibers it innervates; one muscle has many motor units.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The crossed extensor reflex:
questions.explanation: The crossed extensor reflex is a polysynaptic reflex that provides postural support when one limb withdraws from pain. It activates ipsilateral extensors and contralateral flexors to maintain balance and prevent falling.
questions.keyConcept: Crossed extensor reflex: polysynaptic, supports body weight during withdrawal, reciprocal inhibition involved.
options: Provides a typical example of servoassist function.
Is due to stimulation of nuclear bag fibers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding the crossed extensor reflex, which Sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: The crossed extensor reflex is elicited by CONTRALATERAL (not ipsilateral) painful stimulus. The reflex is polysynaptic, has a longer latency than stretch reflex, and involves intersegmental interneurons.
questions.keyConcept: Crossed extensor: activated by contralateral painful stimulus via polysynaptic interneuronal pathways.
options: Has a longer latency than the stretch reflex.
Is elicited by ipsilateral painful stimulus.
An intersegmental interneuron is involved in this reflex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: +ve Babinski sign is NOT present in:
questions.explanation: A positive Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of hallux with fanning) is normal in infants before age 1 year due to immature corticospinal tracts. It indicates UMN lesion in adults. It IS present in LMNL, chronic UMNL, deep sleep, and coma.
questions.keyConcept: Babinski positive = UMN lesion in adults; normal in infants <1 year; negative in LMN lesions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following reflexes is correctly paired with its receptor?
questions.explanation: The stretch reflex is correctly paired with the muscle spindle as its receptor. Autogenic inhibition involves the Golgi tendon organ, and reciprocal inhibition also involves the Golgi tendon organ or muscle spindle depending on the pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Stretch reflex: muscle spindle receptor; inverse stretch reflex: Golgi tendon organ.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sensory impulses from spindles of a stretched muscle could antagonistic muscles by:
questions.explanation: Sensory impulses from muscle spindles activate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that inhibit alpha motor neurons of antagonistic muscles. This is the basis of reciprocal inhibition during voluntary movement.
questions.keyConcept: Reciprocal inhibition: spindle afferents activate inhibitory interneurons that suppress antagonist motor neurons.
options: Directly inhibiting γ-motor neurons of the antagonistic muscles
Directly inhibiting the α -motor neurons of the antagonistic musce
Inhibiting the transmitter release from the central terminals of afferents from the spindles of the antagonistic muscles

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The receptor for the stretch reflex is the:
questions.explanation: The muscle spindle is the receptor for the stretch reflex. When stretched, intrafusal fibers detect the change and trigger a monosynaptic reflex that causes the muscle to contract, resisting the stretch.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: sensory organ detecting stretch; mediates stretch reflex to maintain muscle length.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Muscle spindles:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are found in virtually all skeletal muscles, not just large ones. They consist of a few intrafusal muscle fibers (nuclear bag and chain types) surrounded by a capsule, NOT extrafusal fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles: present in all muscles; contain intrafusal fibers (not extrafusal); detect stretch.
options: Are found in all skeletal muscles
Are found only in large skeletal muscles
Consist of small numbers of extrafusal muscle fibers
Consist of a large number of extrafusal muscle fibers

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Babinski sign is NOT present in:
questions.explanation: Babinski sign is characteristically absent in extrapyramidal lesions (like Parkinson's) because these affect the basal ganglia, not the corticospinal tracts. It IS present in pyramidal (UMN) lesions, deep sleep, and coma.
questions.keyConcept: Babinski: UMN lesion (+), Extrapyramidal lesion (-), LMN lesion (-), normal infant (-).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Physiologically, an intact innervated muscle can normally be made to contract by stimulation of which of the following neurons innervating that muscle?
questions.explanation: Alpha motor neurons directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers and are the final common pathway for muscle contraction. Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal fibers and adjust spindle sensitivity but cannot directly cause visible muscle contraction.
questions.keyConcept: α-motor neurons: final pathway for skeletal muscle contraction; γ-motor neurons: adjust spindle sensitivity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The muscle spindle remains capable of responding to stretch even the muscle is contracting. This is because of:
questions.explanation: During muscle contraction, alpha motor neurons activate extrafusal fibers while gamma motor neurons simultaneously contract intrafusal fibers, keeping the spindle taut and sensitive to stretch even during contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-gamma coactivation maintains spindle sensitivity during muscle contraction.
options: presence of stretch receptors in the tendon
co-activation of α- and γ-motor neurons

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A reflex arc includes:
questions.explanation: A reflex arc requires at minimum a sensory receptor, a sensory neuron, at least one synapse in the CNS, and an efferent motor neuron. This means at least two sets of sequential neurons (afferent and efferent).
questions.keyConcept: Reflex arc components: receptor → afferent neuron → CNS integration → efferent neuron → effector.
options: At least two sets of sequential neurons
At least two sequential sets of central synapses
At least two types of sensory receptors
At least two types of efferent neurons

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The receptor for the inverse stretch reflex is:
questions.explanation: The Golgi tendon organ (GTO) is the receptor for the inverse stretch reflex. When tension becomes excessive, GTO activation causes autogenic inhibition, preventing muscle damage by causing relaxation.
questions.keyConcept: Inverse stretch reflex: Golgi tendon organ → Ib afferents → inhibition of alpha motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Muscle contraction in response to maintained stretch is initiated by sensory inputs from:
questions.explanation: Nuclear bag fibers (type Ia afferents) detect the velocity and degree of muscle stretch and initiate the stretch reflex. Nuclear chain fibers contribute to static sensitivity. Golgi tendon organs detect tension, not stretch per se.
questions.keyConcept: Nuclear bag fibers: dynamic stretch detection; nuclear chain fibers: static stretch detection.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Increased γ-motor neuron discharge stimulates muscle spindles
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate the contractile ends of intrafusal fibers. When stimulated, they contract the peripheral (polar) regions, stretching the central non-contractile region where sensory endings lie, increasing their discharge.
questions.keyConcept: γ-motor neurons contract intrafusal polar regions, stretching central sensory region, increasing spindle output.
options: Produces stretch of the extrafusal muscle fibers
Causes stretch of the peripheral regions of the intrafusal fibers
Causes stretch of the central region of the intrafusal fibers
Stimulates directly the sensory fibers innervating muscle spindles

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about the reticular formation is correct?
Has a sleep center in its upper part.
Non-specifically activates the whole cortex, mainly directly.
Its activity is inhibited by the medullary reticular formation.
questions.explanation: The reticular formation has a sleep center in the lower pons/medulla (not upper part). The medullary RF is inhibitory (not excitatory) to cortex. The RAS (in midbrain/pons) non-specifically activates cortex mainly via thalamus. These are the correct relationships for understanding ARAS function.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation: pontine/midbrain RAS activates cortex; medullary RF inhibits cortex; sleep center in lower brainstem.
questions.modelAnswer: Correct statement: The reticular activating system (RAS) non-specifically activates the whole cortex, mainly indirectly through thalamic relay nuclei. The medullary reticular formation provides inhibitory projections to cortex. Sleep-promoting centers are located in the lower brainstem (medulla/lower pons) near the raphe nuclei.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Medullary reticular formation is stimulated by:
questions.explanation: The medullary reticular formation receives excitatory input from the primary motor cortex via corticofugal fibers. It does not receive direct input from basal ganglia or cerebellum; those project to brainstem nuclei that then influence medullary RF.
questions.keyConcept: Medullary RF receives cortical input; basal ganglia/cerebellum influence it indirectly via brainstem nuclei.
options: Gamma motor neurons of spinal cord anterior horn.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true about the reticular formation:
questions.explanation: The excitatory component of reticular formation is located in the PONS, not the medulla. The medullary RF is inhibitory. All other statements about ARAS being excitatory, pontine part facilitating spinal cord, and reticular formation being stimulated by cortical/sensory inputs are true.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation: pontine part = excitatory (ARAS); medullary part = inhibitory.
options: Its excitatory component is located in the pons.
Its medullary component is inhibitory to all cortical areas.
Its excitatory components constitutes the ARAS.
Its pontine part is excitatory to spinal cord motor neurons.
It is stimulated by both of Corticofugal and sensory fibers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT involved in decreasing the activity of the pontine reticular formation?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus is a facilitatory center that INCREASES pontine reticular formation activity, not decreases it. Cortical inhibitory areas, medullary RF, basal ganglia, and corticofugal fibers all decrease pontine RF activity.
questions.keyConcept: Red nucleus facilitates pontine RF; cortical areas, basal ganglia, medullary RF inhibit it.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a character of ARAS:
questions.explanation: The ARAS does NOT receive excitatory impulses from cortical areas; rather, cortical areas excite the ARAS. The ARAS is present in pons/midbrain, indirectly activates cortex, facilitates antigravity muscles, and is responsible for arousal.
questions.keyConcept: ARAS: brainstem system that activates cortex; receives input FROM cortex, not sending to it.
options: Indirectly and directly excites the whole cortex.
Receives excitatory impulses from cortical areas.
Facilitates spinal cord motor neurons of antigravity muscles.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning reticular formation, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Red nucleus and paleocerebellum FACILITATE (not inhibit) the pontine reticular formation. The pontine RF is the excitatory ARAS component. The medullary RF is inhibitory to antigravity muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine RF: facilitatory, activated by red nucleus/paleocerebellum. Medullary RF: inhibitory to antigravity muscles.
options: It receives impulses from various somatic and special sense pathways.
Its inhibitory motor part inhibits the spinal cord motor neurons of antigravity muscles.
Its facilitatory motor part excites both the cortex and the spinal cord.
Its intrinsic activities characterized by diffuse electric activity of all its components.
Red nucleus and paleocerebellum inhibit its pontine component.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning reticular formation, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation is NOT responsible for perception and localization of fast pain - that is a function of the specific somatosensory pathways (spinothalamic tract). RF is responsible for arousal, pain modulation, sleep/wake cycles, and motor control.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain localization = specific sensory pathways; RF handles arousal, modulation, and autonomic functions.
options: It excites all parts of cortex through ARAS.
It is a link between higher and lower CNS centers.
It is responsible for perception and localization of fast pain.
It is responsible for brain electrical activity.
Its descending motor facilitatory component plays a role in body support.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Secondary evoked potential is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Secondary evoked potential is a diffuse, generalized wave recorded after an initial localized wave. Primary evoked potentials are localized to specific areas. Secondary waves are due to non-specific thalamic nuclei activity and are recorded during mental activity.
questions.keyConcept: Primary EP: localized; Secondary EP: diffuse, generalized, from non-specific thalamic nuclei.
options: Localized to a specific cortical area.
Consists of a small +ve followed by a small –ve wave.
Similar to beta waves of EEG.
Due to stimulation of non-specific thalamic nuclei.
Recorded when the person shows mental activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Electroencephalogram:
questions.explanation: The EEG represents summation of excitatory (EPSP) and inhibitory (IPSP) postsynaptic potentials in cortical neurons. It is recorded in awake persons, not anesthetized. Theta waves appear during relaxed states; beta waves during alert states.
questions.keyConcept: EEG = summation of cortical EPSPs/IPSPs; alpha in relaxed wakefulness; beta in alertness; theta in drowsiness.
options: Represents summation of EPSP & IPSP in brain neurons.
Theta waves dominate in adult during awake state with mental rest.
Beta waves are recorded in light sleep.
A diffuse generalized wave is recorded after an initial localized small wave.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Brain waves:
questions.explanation: Desynchronized, low voltage, high frequency (beta) waves are recorded when RAS is activated during alertness. Paradoxical sleep shows similar waves. Alpha waves dominate relaxed wakefulness. Delta waves are slow, high voltage seen in deep sleep. Gamma waves are high frequency associated with cognitive processing.
questions.keyConcept: Beta = RAS activation/alertness; Alpha = relaxed wake; Theta = drowsiness/children; Delta = deep sleep; Gamma = cognition.
options: Regular synchronized alpha waves are recorded in paradoxical sleep.
Desynchronized, low voltage, high frequency waves are recorded due to activation of RAS.
Highest voltage low frequency waves are recorded in adults during awake relaxed state.
Intrinsic activity of reticular formation produces beta waves.
Gamma waves are recorded in deep sleep.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The EEG wave recorded in high mental activity, hyperaroused state is:
questions.explanation: Beta waves (13-30 Hz, 25μV, irregular, desynchronized) are recorded during high mental activity and hyperaroused states. Alpha waves dominate relaxed wakefulness; theta waves appear in drowsiness and children; delta waves in deep sleep; gamma waves (30-80 Hz) are associated with consciousness but are very low voltage.
questions.keyConcept: Beta waves: alert, active thinking; alpha: relaxed closed eyes; theta: drowsy/children; delta: sleep.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The EEG wave recorded in children is:
questions.explanation: Theta waves (4-7 Hz, 100μV, regular, synchronized) are prominent in children and adults during drowsiness. Alpha waves dominate in adults at rest; beta in alertness; delta in deep sleep; gamma in intensive cognitive tasks.
questions.keyConcept: Theta waves: dominant in children; appear in adult drowsiness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: β waves of EEG are:
questions.explanation: Beta waves are faster than alpha (13-30 Hz vs 8-13 Hz) and are recorded during alert, active states, not in relaxed or sleeping states. They disappear (replaced by alpha) when a person relaxes with eyes closed. They are NOT character of relaxed awake state, children, or paradoxical sleep.
questions.keyConcept: Beta waves: alert/active mental state, faster than alpha, low voltage, desynchronized.
options: Faster than α waves, but slower than δ waves.
Disappear when the person becomes alert.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding Evoked brain potentials:
questions.explanation: Evoked potentials represent summation of EPSPs and IPSPs in brain neurons in response to stimuli. They are used for brain mapping, recorded in conscious individuals, and consist of primary (localized) followed by secondary (diffuse) waves. They are NOT due to RAS activity.
questions.keyConcept: Evoked potentials: cortical response to sensory input; EPSP/IPSP summation; primary (specific) then secondary (diffuse).
options: It is used for mapping of the brain.
It is recorded in a conscious person.
It consists of a primary diffuse wave followed by a secondary localized wave.
It is due to activity of RAS.
It represents summation of excitatory and inhibitory potentials in brain neurons

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following sentences about sleep and arousal is true:
questions.explanation: Orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake switching by modulating brainstem nuclei activity. Posterior hypothalamus promotes wakefulness; cholinergic neurons induce arousal; serotonergic and noradrenergic neurons promote REM sleep at different sites.
questions.keyConcept: Orexin regulates sleep-wake balance; posterior hypothalamus = wakefulness; cholinergic = arousal; serotonergic/noradrenergic = REM.
options: Posterior hypothalamus is a Non-REM sleep center.
Cholinergic neurons of upper brain stem induce arousal.
Serotonergic brain stem neurons induce REM sleep.
Suprachasmatic nucleus is a REM sleep center.
Orexin hormone of the hypothalamus regulates brain stem nuclei activity and switches the activity between seep and arousal.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: REM sleep differs from Non-REM sleep in:
questions.explanation: REM sleep is characterized by low voltage desynchronized waves (like wakefulness), vivid dreams, penile erection, and irregular HR/BP. Non-REM has synchronized waves, longer duration early in night, and increased GH. Both have different durations throughout sleep.
questions.keyConcept: REM: desynchronized EEG, dreams, irregular vitals, low arousal threshold; non-REM: synchronized EEG, longer early cycle.
options: Has longer duration in the sleep cycles.
Low voltage desynchronized brain waves are recorded during it.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sleep, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus PROMOTES wakefulness and arousal, not sleep. These nuclei are part of the ascending activating system. Sleep may be due to synaptic fatigue, active inhibition of RAS, or sleep-inducing substances.
questions.keyConcept: Raphe magnus and locus coeruleus = wakefulness/REM-on neurons; NOT sleep centers.
options: It helps brain rest and brain plasticity.
It may be due to synaptic fatigue of RAS neurons.
It may be due to active inhibition of RAS by sleep centers.
It may be due to increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus brain stem nuclei.
It may be due to accumulation of sleep inducing lipids or peptide in the CSF.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compared to REM sleep, Non-REM sleep is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Non-REM sleep is characterized by increased growth hormone secretion (especially in early sleep cycles), synchronized high-amplitude slow waves, decreased muscle tone, and autonomic stability. REM sleep has irregular HR/BP, dreams, decreased muscle tone, and no GH increase.
questions.keyConcept: Non-REM: GH secretion, synchronized EEG, muscle relaxation; REM: dreams, desynchronized EEG, atonia.
options: Recording of high frequency, low voltage, desynchronized brain waves.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Paradoxical sleep is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Paradoxical (REM) sleep includes rapid eye movements and movement of finger/toe muscles, occurs later in sleep cycles (not at start), and has 4 stages only in non-REM. Vitals are irregular, not markedly decreased. REM is important for mental restitution.
questions.keyConcept: REM sleep: rapid eye movements, muscle twitches, irregular vitals, dreaming, mental restoration.
options: Occurs at the start of sleep cycle.
Movement of eye, finger and toe muscles.
Marked decrease in blood pressure & heart rate.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a REM sleep center:
questions.explanation: The locus coeruleus (noradrenergic) and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei (cholinergic) are REM sleep centers. Raphe nucleus promotes sleep but is more related to non-REM. Anterior hypothalamus is sleep-promoting; suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythm.
questions.keyConcept: REM sleep centers: locus coeruleus (noradrenergic), LDT/PPT (cholinergic).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a neurotransmitter for REM sleep:
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter for REM sleep, released by cholinergic neurons in the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus. Norepinephrine and serotonin are associated with wakefulness and non-REM sleep.
questions.keyConcept: REM sleep: cholinergic neurotransmission; serotonin/norepinephrine: wakefulness/non-REM.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of the prefrontal association area:
questions.explanation: Language comprehension is a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the prefrontal association area. The prefrontal area handles working memory, decision-making, personality, abstract thinking, and storage of vocalization programs.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal functions: executive function, working memory, personality, decision-making. Language = temporal/parietal areas.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning speech, all are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Anomic aphasia is due to lesion in the angular gyrus (not auditory cortex), which connects visual, auditory, and tactile information. The patient can comprehend but cannot name objects. Broca's aphasia is characterized by sparse, effortful speech, not excessive speech.
questions.keyConcept: Anomic aphasia: angular gyrus lesion; can't name objects despite comprehension.
options: Sensory aphasia occurs due to defect in visual association area, auditory association area or Wernicke’s area.
Expressive aphasia occurs due to lesion in Broca’s area or Exner’s area.
Anomic aphasia is due to lesion in and around auditory cortex.
In anomic aphasia, the patient cannot give name for seen pictures and words.
Aphasia occurs only in case of lesion in the categorical hemisphere.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Aphasia:
questions.explanation: Aphasia is a language disorder (not articulation), often fluent in Wernicke's aphasia. It is not due to LMN lesions. Broca's aphasia is characterized by non-fluent, effortful, meaningful speech (not meaningless). The key distinction is language vs articulation.
questions.keyConcept: Aphasia = language disorder (not motor); Wernicke = fluent aphasia; Broca = non-fluent aphasia.
options: Is an abnormal speech due to defect in articulation.
Is of fluent type due to lesion in Wernicke’s area.
May be due to lower motor neuron lesion of vocalization muscles.
Is expressive in type due to lesion in auditory association cortex.
Broca’s aphasia characterized by excessive meaningless speech.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lesion in frontal lobe speech center produces:
questions.explanation: Lesion in Broca's area (frontal lobe speech center) produces expressive aphasia - difficulty producing speech despite understanding. The patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate. Sensory aphasia (Wernicke's) affects comprehension; motor aphasia affects speech production.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area lesion: expressive (motor) aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Speech centers do NOT include:
questions.explanation: The somatic sensory association area is NOT a primary speech center. Speech requires Wernicke's area, Broca's area, auditory association area, and visual association area for reading. Broca's is in frontal lobe; Wernicke's and auditory areas in temporal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Speech centers: Broca's (frontal), Wernicke's (temporal), auditory/visual association areas. Somatic sensory association is NOT required for speech.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sensory aphasia occurs with lesion in:
questions.explanation: Sensory aphasia occurs with lesion in Wernicke's area or auditory association area, causing poor comprehension and fluent but meaningless speech. Visual pathway lesions cause blindness; Broca's/Exner cause motor aphasia; tongue muscles cause dysarthria.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory aphasia: Wernicke's area/auditory association lesion = fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning learning:
questions.explanation: Sensitization occurs by presynaptic facilitation of sensory neurons. Habituation involves decreased synaptic transmission (not increased calcium) due to less neurotransmitter release. Operant conditioning uses reinforcement, not neutral stimuli. Classical conditioning pairs unconditioned and conditioned stimuli. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant.
questions.keyConcept: Habituation: decreased response to repeated benign stimulus. Sensitization: enhanced response via presynaptic facilitation.
options: Habituation is due to increase intracellular calcium leading to augmented response.
Operant conditioning occurs by inducing a response to a neutral stimulus.
Classical conditioning occurs by stimulation of reward and punishment centers.
-ve operant conditioning means adding of something to induce learning of a specific task or behavior

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Motor aphasia occurs with lesion in:
questions.explanation: Motor aphasia (Broca's aphasia) occurs with lesion in Exner/Broca's area in the frontal lobe. Primary motor area causes paralysis, not aphasia. Auditory association/Wernicke's areas cause sensory aphasia. Angular gyrus causes conduction aphasia.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's/Exner's area: motor aphasia (difficulty producing speech). Wernicke's: sensory aphasia (difficulty understanding).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning Learning:
questions.explanation: In classical conditioning, the conditioned stimulus (neutral) becomes associated with the unconditioned stimulus to produce a conditioned response. Habituation is decreased response to benign stimuli. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant to increase behavior. Associative learning occurs when two stimuli are paired.
questions.keyConcept: Classical conditioning: CS paired with US to produce CR. Habituation: decreased response to benign stimulus.
options: In habituation, a repeated benign stimulus produces gradual loss of response.
Associative learning is present when a noxious stimulus occurs with a benign one.
Pairing of stimuli is a type of simple learning.
Adding a reward to decrease a certain behavior is a +ve reinforcement.
In classical conditioning, an unconditioned stimulus can produce a certain response when paired with a neutral conditioned stimulus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding dysarthria, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dysarthria due to Wernicke's area lesion would cause receptive aphasia, not dysarthria. Wernicke's area controls language comprehension. Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder affecting articulation due to UMN/LMN lesions to speech muscles, not a cortical language area lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Dysarthria = motor speech disorder (articulation); Wernicke's area = receptive aphasia (comprehension).
options: It is a speech abnormality due to defect in articulation.
It occurs in UMNL & LMNL affecting speech muscles.
Is of slow monotonous type in Parkinsonism.
Is of spastic type due to lesion in Wernicke’s area.
Is of ataxic staccato type in neocerebellar syndrome

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which sentence is NOT correct for long-term potentiation:
questions.explanation: LTP (long-term potentiation) is primarily involved in hippocampal learning, not cerebellar learning. The cerebellum uses a different mechanism involving LTD (long-term depression) for motor learning. LTP does involve glutamate/NMDA receptors, Ca++ increases, protein synthesis, and new connections.
questions.keyConcept: LTP: hippocampal learning (memory); LTD: cerebellar learning (motor). Both involve glutamate receptors.
options: A rapid repeated brief stimulation leads to a persistent enhancement of response.
Glutamate transmitter and its NMDA receptors may play a role.
Increase Ca++ in pre and post-synaptic neurons may play a role.
Protein synthesis, growth and increased neuronal connections are possible mechanisms.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In memory:
questions.explanation: Episodic memory (remembering events) is stored in hippocampus and neocortex. Explicit memory IS conscious recall (not implicit). Implicit memory includes priming and procedural memory stored in basal ganglia/cerebellum. Semantic memory is general knowledge, not events.
questions.keyConcept: Explicit/declarative: conscious, hippocampus/neocortex. Implicit/non-declarative: unconscious, basal ganglia/cerebellum.
options: Implicit memory is the conscious recall of information.
Explicit memory is stored in basal ganglia and cerebellum.
Explicit memory types include priming and procedural memory.
Episodic memory is stored in the hippocampus and neocortex.
Semantic memory is the recall of events and experiences.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Short-term memory is:
questions.explanation: Short-term memory involves transient synaptic modifications like increased neurotransmitter release. It is limited capacity, stored in hippocampal/prefrontal areas initially (not neocortex directly). It requires hours for cortical storage. Gene activation is for long-term memory.
questions.keyConcept: Short-term memory: transient synaptic changes, limited capacity (7±2 items), hippocampal. Long-term: structural changes, unlimited.
options: Stored after 2 hours from getting the information.
Brain capacity for it is unlimited.
Encoded and stored in the neocortex.
Due to transient synaptic modifications such as increased release of neurotransmitters.
Involves gene activation and protein synthesis

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Long-term memory is:
questions.explanation: Long-term memory involves gene activation, protein synthesis, and structural synaptic changes (not transient neurotransmitter release). Capacity is unlimited. Stored in neocortex eventually (not frontal lobe only). Hippocampus is for consolidation, not permanent storage.
questions.keyConcept: LTM: gene activation, protein synthesis, new synapses; unlimited capacity; stored in neocortex.
options: Stored immediately after getting the information.
Brain capacity for it is limited.
Encoded in hippocampus and stored in the frontal lobe.
Due to transient synaptic modifications such as increased release of neurotransmitters.
Involves gene activation and protein synthesis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true regarding consolidation of memory:
questions.explanation: Consolidation takes much longer than 5 minutes - it can take hours to days. Consolidation is the conversion of STM to LTM through synaptic changes and takes time for structural modifications. Completed in 5 minutes is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Memory consolidation: conversion of STM to LTM; takes hours-days; requires protein synthesis.
options: It is the conversion of short-term memory to a long-term one.
Represents the time needed for the structural and functional synaptic changes to take place.
Increases and fastens by focusing and rehearsal.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mechanisms of long-term memory do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Transient synaptic modifications are characteristic of SHORT-term memory, not long-term. LTM mechanisms include increased presynaptic terminals, structural/functional synaptic changes, new synapses, and gene activation/protein synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: STM: transient changes. LTM: structural changes, new synapses, gene activation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The primary role of amygdala in memory is:
questions.explanation: The amygdala processes the emotional significance of memories (fear conditioning, emotional tagging) but does not store semantic memory, initiate synaptic changes, or handle short-term memory operation. The hippocampus handles consolidation and storage.
questions.keyConcept: Amygdala: emotional component of memory (fear, emotional tagging). Hippocampus: consolidation and declarative memory.
options: Processing and remembering the emotional component of memories.
Initiation of synaptic changes needed for memory storage.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Consolidation of memory increases by:
questions.explanation: Sleep (especially REM sleep) enhances memory consolidation through synaptic reorganization. Anesthesia, concussion, and electroshock impair consolidation. Mental fatigue reduces consolidation efficiency.
questions.keyConcept: REM sleep enhances memory consolidation by promoting synaptic plasticity and memory transfer to cortex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Consolidation of memory decreases by:
questions.explanation: REM sleep is critical for memory consolidation. Lack of REM sleep impairs consolidation. Interesting information, rehearsal, mental rest, and quiet sleep all enhance consolidation.
questions.keyConcept: REM sleep is essential for memory consolidation; deprivation impairs learning and memory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Habituation:
questions.explanation: Habituation is decreased response to repeated benign stimuli due to decreased neurotransmitter release (not inactivation of postsynaptic Ca++ channels). It does not involve new synapse formation or operant conditioning (that's sensitization).
questions.keyConcept: Habituation: decreased transmitter release from sensory neurons → decreased response to benign stimuli.
options: Is the gradual increase in response in presence of a repeated stimulus.
Explained by gradual inactivation of Ca++ channels in the postsynaptic neuron.
Leads to the formation of new synapses.
Is due to gradual decrease in the neurotransmitter release in the involved pathway.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true about sensitization:
questions.explanation: Sensitization can last much longer than 60 seconds - it can persist for days in long-term sensitization. It does involve serotonergic facilitation, operates in both short and long-term memory, and is associated with noxious stimuli paired to benign ones.
questions.keyConcept: Sensitization: enhanced response to stimuli after noxious input; serotonergic facilitation; can be short or long-term.
options: A prolonged augmented response occurs when a noxious stimulus paired to a benign stimulus.
It is due to serotonin-induced facilitation.
It continues up to 60 seconds after removal of the stimulus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Post-tetanic facilitation:
questions.explanation: Post-tetanic facilitation is explained by Ca++ accumulation in the presynaptic terminal after rapid stimulation, leading to increased neurotransmitter release. It is not gradual loss (that's habituation), not continuation after stimulus removal (that's post-tetanic potentiation), and not basis of classical conditioning.
questions.keyConcept: Post-tetanic facilitation: Ca2+ accumulation → increased transmitter release → enhanced response during tetanus.
options: Is a gradual loss of response to a repeated benign stimulus.
The postsynaptic response continues as long as the presynaptic stimulation is maintained.
Explained by accumulation of Ca++ in the presynaptic neuron upon rapid short-term stimulation.
Is associated with decrease postsynaptic response after removal of presynaptic stimulation.
Is the basis of classical conditioning.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In long-term depression:
questions.explanation: LTD (long-term depression) involves slow, prolonged low-frequency stimulation that decreases synaptic strength. LTP involves rapid repeated tetanic stimulation that increases strength. Sensitization involves noxious stimuli causing facilitation. Classic conditioning involves CS-US pairing.
questions.keyConcept: LTD: low-frequency stimulation → decreased transmission (cerebellum). LTP: high-frequency → increased transmission (hippocampus).
options: A rapid repeated brief stimulation leads to a persistent enhancement of response.
A slow, prolonged, low frequency stimulation leads to decrease strength of synaptic transmission.
A rapid tetanizing presynaptic stimulation leads to continuation of postsynaptic response after removal of the stimulus.
A noxious stimulus leads to presynaptic facilitation of a habituated pathway.
A continuous benign stimulus leads to gradual increase in response.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lateral nuclei of hypothalamus are NOT involved in:
questions.explanation: Heat gain is a function of the posterior hypothalamus (not lateral). The lateral hypothalamus handles feeding, thirst, orexin release, rage, and approach motivation. The ventromedial nucleus is the satiety center.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral hypothalamus: feeding, thirst, orexin, rage. Posterior hypothalamus: heat conservation/gain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Functions of the limbic system do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Olfactory perception and discrimination is primarily a function of the olfactory bulb and temporal lobe, not the limbic system. The limbic system controls feeding, maternal/sexual behaviors, emotions, water balance, and motivations.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic functions: emotions, motivation, feeding, sexual behavior, memory. Olfaction: olfactory bulb/piriform cortex.
options: Control of feeding, maternal & sexual behaviors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true about the Amygdala:
questions.explanation: The amygdala is NOT the area for consolidation of memory - that is the hippocampus. The amygdala processes emotional responses and emotional components of memories. Lesion leads to hypoactive emotional response, not hyperphagia. Stimulation causes rage.
questions.keyConcept: Amygdala: emotional processing of memories. Hippocampus: memory consolidation. Different structures.
options: Is involved in processing of the emotional components of memories.
Is involved in processing of the emotional responses to odors.
Its lesion leads to hyperphagia and omniphagia.
Its stimulation leads to rage and aggression.
Is the area for consolidation of memory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The hypothalamus performs all of the following functions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus controls autonomic functions, pituitary regulation, temperature, and appetite - but NOT voluntary movements. Voluntary movements are controlled by the motor cortex and basal ganglia. Hypothalamus handles autonomic and homeostatic functions.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamus: autonomic, endocrine, temperature, appetite. Motor cortex: voluntary movement.
options: Regulation of anterior and posterior pituitary hormonal secretion.
Control of appetite and food intake.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding the hypothalamus:
questions.explanation: Heat gain center is in the POSTERIOR hypothalamus (not anterior). Anterior hypothalamus is for heat loss. Satiety center (ventromedial) does not have intrinsic activity - it responds to signals. Suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythms, not body activities synchronization in that context.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus: heat loss. Posterior hypothalamus: heat gain. Ventromedial: satiety. Lateral: feeding.
options: Heat gain center is present in the anterior hypothalamus.
Ventromedial nuclei synchronize body activities according to dark-light cycles.
Posterior hypothalamus function as a sleep center.
Anterior hypothalamic nuclei play a role in all of sleep, heat loss, parasympathetic activity and sexual drive.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text:
Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
I. Pacinian corpuscle.
II. Meissner’s corpuscle.
III. Ruffini’ corpuscle.
questions.explanation: Ruffini's corpuscles (type II slowly adapting mechanoreceptors) are proprioceptors in joints and skin. Pacinian corpuscles are vibration/pressure receptors. Meissner's corpuscles are light touch in dermal papillae. Muscle spindles are the primary proprioceptors in muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptors: muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, Ruffini's (joints). Vibration: Pacinian. Light touch: Meissner's.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a receptor for vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles (type V rapidly adapting) are the primary vibration and deep pressure receptors. They are located deep in the dermis and respond to high-frequency vibration. Meissner's is light touch, Ruffini's is stretch, Merkel's is pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle: vibration (500 Hz), deep pressure, rapidly adapting, deep dermis.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is NOT a character of Meissner’s corpuscle:
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscle has Schwann cells arranged in horizontal stacks (not spirally). The nerve fiber runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks. Merkel's disc has nerve fibers running spirally. Meissner's is encapsulated, in dermal papillae, and responds to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: Schwann cells in horizontal stacks, nerve fibers spiral; light touch receptor in dermal papillae.
options: It is an encapsulated nerve ending.
It is present in dermal papillae.
The Schwann cells are arranged in two cores.
The nerve fibers run spirally between the Schwann cells.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All about muscle spindle true except:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen fibers primarily). The capsule encloses the spindle but the internal structure is muscle fiber-based. They are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, have gamma efferents, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel with extrafusal fibers, contains intrafusal muscle fibers, encapsulated, gamma innervation.
options: Present in parallel with sk. Muscle fibers.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Krause end bulb, all true except:
questions.explanation: Krause end bulbs have spherical structures with a gelatinous core, function as cold receptors, and are found in conjunctiva and oral cavity. They are mechanoreceptors. The statement about flattened Teloglia cells is incorrect - they have a different structure.
questions.keyConcept: Krause end bulb: cold receptor, mechanoreceptor, gelatinous core, found in conjunctiva and mouth.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of muscle spindle:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are innervated by both afferent (Ia, II) and efferent (gamma) nerve fibers. They contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen), are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, respond to stretch, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel arrangement, intrafusal fibers, afferent + efferent innervation, stretch receptor.
options: Present In series with muscle fibers.
Innervated by afferent & efferent nerve fiber.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pacinian corpuscle:
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric layers of Teloglia (not Schwann cells arranged transversely). They are located deep in the dermis (not dermal papillae), are encapsulated (not non-capsulated), and the nerve fiber runs centrally (not in spiral).
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle: concentric Teloglia layers, deep dermis, vibration receptor, encapsulated.
options: Lies in dermal papillae of skin.
Nerve fibers run in spiral coarse.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following receptors are mechanoreceptors?
questions.explanation: All of these - Merkel's disc, Meissner's corpuscle, and Bounet's plexus (a free nerve ending network) are mechanoreceptors. They transduce mechanical stimuli into neural signals. Merkel's = pressure, Meissner's = light touch, Bounet's = slowly adapting stretch receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanoreceptors: Merkel's (pressure), Meissner's (touch), Bounet's plexus (stretch). All detect mechanical stimuli.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The sensory nerve enters the Meissner’s corpuscle from:
questions.explanation: In Meissner's corpuscle, the sensory nerve enters from the SIDE (laterally), not from the lower part or central core. The nerve fiber then runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks within the corpuscle.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: sensory nerve enters from side; nerve fibers spiral between Schwann cell stacks.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Free nerve endings are widely distributed in
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are the simplest sensory receptors and are widely distributed throughout the body including epidermis, cornea, mucous membranes of visceral organs, and serous membranes. They detect pain, temperature, and crude touch.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings: most widely distributed receptor; detect pain, temperature, crude touch; in epidermis, cornea, viscera.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: What do free nerve endings respond to?
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings respond to noxious (painful), thermal, and crude touch stimuli. They are polymodal receptors capable of detecting multiple stimulus types. Different fiber types (A-delta for pain/temperature, C for pain) mediate these responses.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings: polymodal - respond to painful, thermal, and tactile stimuli via Aδ and C fibers.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: What is the site of Merkel’s tactile disc?
questions.explanation: Merkel's tactile discs are found in BOTH hairy and non-hairy skin, particularly in the deep layers of epidermis of palms, soles, and at transitional zones between hairy and non-hairy skin. They are slowly adapting touch receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Merkel's disc: deep epidermis of palms/soles and hairy-non hairy skin transitions; slowly adapting touch receptor.
options: Deep layers of the epidermis of the palmer surfaces of hands and planter surfaces of feet
Transitional sites between hairy & non-hairy skin

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pacinian corpuscles are found in
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are found in deep tissues including dermis and hypodermis, as well as mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder, and other viscera. They detect deep pressure and vibration. Their wide distribution reflects their role in detecting deep mechanical stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles: deep dermis, hypodermis, mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder - deep pressure/vibration.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lumbar spinal cord has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains a large amount of grey matter (lower motor neurons for legs) relative to white matter (mostly descending tracts passing through). It has lateral horns for sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar cord: large grey matter (LMN for lower limb), small white/grey ratio, lateral horns present.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of thoracic level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The thoracic spinal cord has 4 horns (anterior, posterior, and lateral on each side). The lateral horns contain sympathetic preganglionic neurons. It is intermediate in size, oval-shaped. Cervical and lumbar enlargements are larger.
questions.keyConcept: Thoracic cord: 4 horns including lateral horns (sympathetic), intermediate size, oval shape.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has the LARGEST white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains extensive ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) tracts to/from the brain for the upper limbs and body. It is rounded in shape and large in size.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord: largest white/grey ratio (many tracts), rounded, large size.
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: About spinal nerve all true except:
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - large neurons for proprioception, medium for touch, small for pain. Lateral division of dorsal root carries pain and temperature; medial division carries proprioception and fine touch. Thick myelinated fibers carry proprioceptive information.
questions.keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable sizes (large=proprioception, small=pain); lateral = pain/temp; medial = touch/proprioception.
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion:
questions.explanation: DRG neurons are of variable size (pseudounipolar neurons with different diameters). The ganglion is located on the dorsal root OUTSIDE the CNS (not inside), surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. It is not located at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: pseudounipolar neurons of variable size, encapsulated, located on dorsal root outside CNS.
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Nerve cells of dorsal root ganglia are characterized by:
questions.explanation: DRG cells are pseudounipolar with multiple processes (one peripheral, one central). They have eccentric nuclei, are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers, and are surrounded by satellite glial cells (not Schwann cells around the cell body itself).
questions.keyConcept: DRG cells: pseudounipolar, multiple processes, eccentric nucleus, satellite cells, myelinated + unmyelinated fibers.
options: Associated with myelinated & unmyelinated nerve fibers.
Have shwann cells around its cell bodies.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text:
Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
I. It is rich in connective tissue cells.
II. It is soft jelly like.
III. It has grey matter and white matter.
questions.explanation: CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft, jelly-like (due to high water content), and has both grey matter (cell bodies) and white matter (myelinated fibers).
questions.keyConcept: CNS: poor in CT, soft/jelly-like (high water), has grey (neurons) and white (myelinated) matter.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Dura matter characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Dura mater is a fibrous, avascular layer (contains few blood vessels). It forms the outermost meninx. Arachnoid has trabeculae; pia is vascular; arachnoid barrier layer is cellular. Dura's toughness comes from collagen fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: tough outer meninx, fibrous, relatively avascular; attached to periosteum of skull/vertebrae.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Concerning the pia matter, which of the following statements is true:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is highly vascular (contains blood vessels that penetrate to supply superficial brain tissue). It is the innermost meninx, in direct contact with brain. Arachnoid contains spaces (subarachnoid) for CSF, not pia. Dura contains venous sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater: highly vascular, innermost meninx, follows brain contours closely.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (in grey matter) have numerous short branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (in white matter) have few long unbranched processes. Both types express GFAP and have foot processes on blood vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: grey matter, numerous short processes. Fibrous astrocytes: white matter, few long processes.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Tanycytes line which of the following:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the third ventricle and other ventricular surfaces, particularly in the hypothalamus. They have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and are involved in neuroendocrine regulation.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes: specialized ependymal cells lining 3rd ventricle, transport molecules between brain and CSF.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The apical surface of ependymal Cells has:
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surface that help circulate CSF. They also have microvilli but cilia are the distinguishing feature. The ciliary movement helps propel CSF through the ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lining ventricles; cilia circulate CSF.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the followings have choroid Plexus EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct connects the 3rd and 4th ventricles but has NO choroid plexus - it is just a narrow channel through the midbrain. Choroid plexus is present in lateral ventricles, 3rd ventricle, and 4th ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Choroid plexus: lateral, 3rd, and 4th ventricles. NOT in cerebral aqueduct (midbrain).

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central canal is lined by:
questions.explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated. This ependymal lining continues throughout the ventricular system. The cilia help circulate CSF within the canal.
questions.keyConcept: Central canal: lined by partially ciliated simple columnar-cuboidal epithelium (ependymal cells).
options: Simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium partially ciliated.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ___ while microglia Is derived from ___:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (neural tube/glial precursors), same as neurons and astrocytes. Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage), making them the only non-ectodermal glial cells in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: neuroectoderm. Microglia: mesoderm (monocyte origin). Astrocytes: neuroectoderm.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following cells Produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons). Schwann cells do this in the PNS. Astrocytes provide support; satellite cells support neurons in ganglia; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin (multiple axons). Schwann cells: PNS myelin (one axon each).

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in injury and disease to phagocytose debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic under normal conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages (phagocytic), mesodermal origin, activated in injury/disease.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: In the CNS Injury, which of the following cells are abundant:
questions.explanation: In CNS injury, astrocytes proliferate (gliosis) to form glial scars, and microglia activate to phagocytose debris. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response. Oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells do not become abundant.
questions.keyConcept: CNS injury response: astrocyte proliferation (gliosis) + microglia activation (phagocytosis).

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved in the blood brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes (specifically their foot processes) are key components of the blood-brain barrier, forming a protective layer around capillaries. They induce endothelial cells to form tight junctions. Ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier, not BBB.
questions.keyConcept: Blood-brain barrier: astrocyte foot processes + tight junction endothelial cells; excludes many substances.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter appears grey because it contains nerve cell bodies (unmyelinated or lightly myelinated). White matter appears white due to myelin on axons. The distribution of myelin determines the distribution of grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter: neuron cell bodies. White matter: myelinated axons. Myelin determines white/grey distribution.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the following a component of Blood CSF barrier:
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by the choroid plexus epithelium (border cells of arachnoid matter - actually choroid plexus cells), not ependymal cells. Ependymal cells line ventricles. The barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries + choroid plexus epithelium with tight junctions.
questions.keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier: choroid plexus epithelium + fenestrated capillaries + tight junctions.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies, glial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of WHITE matter, not grey matter. This is why grey matter appears grey (neuron cell bodies) and white matter appears white (myelin).
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter: cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated fibers. White matter: myelinated axons.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Martinoti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells have axons directed UPWARDS (toward the cortical surface). Their dendrites extend laterally, cell bodies are multipolar (not rounded), and they use various neurotransmitters. They are inhibitory interneurons in the cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells: cortical interneurons with ascending axons; deliver inhibitory signals to superficial layers.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Inner Pyramidal cells are present in layer …. of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called Betz cells when giant) are found in layer V of the motor cortex, not in layers I-IV. Layer V is the internal pyramidal layer. The options I-IV are incorrect - inner pyramidal refers to layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Layer V (internal pyramidal): Betz cells, corticospinal neurons. Layer IV: thalamocortical input.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Giant cells of Betz are present in which layer of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Giant cells of Betz are found in the INNER PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V) of the motor cortex. These are the largest neurons in the CNS and give rise to corticospinal tract fibers. They are characteristic of the primary motor area.
questions.keyConcept: Betz cells: giant pyramidal neurons in layer V of motor cortex; corticospinal tract origin.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cerebral cortex is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Cerebral cortex has both laminar (6 layers) and columnar (functional minicolumns) organization. It has a folded surface (gyri and sulci), varying thickness, different neuron shapes in different layers, and shows plasticity.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex: 6 layers, columnar organization, folded surface, varying thickness, high plasticity.
options: Layers of the same thickness all over the brain

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cells of Cajal are present in
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the MOLECULAR layer of the CEREBRAL cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface. In cerebellum, this layer contains Purkinje cells, not Cajal cells.
questions.keyConcept: Cajal cells: horizontal cells in molecular layer of cerebral cortex; horizontal axon orientation.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the following are layers of cerebral cortex EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Purkinje layer is a layer of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex layers are: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), multiform (VI).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex 6 layers: I molecular, II external granular, III external pyramidal, IV internal granular, V internal pyramidal, VI multiform. Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pia matter is formed of:
questions.explanation: Pia mater is formed of modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal cells) arranged in a thin connective tissue layer. It is not epithelial (not squamous or columnar). The outer surface faces the subarachnoid space, and the inner surface is in contact with brain.
questions.keyConcept: Pia mater: modified fibroblasts (mesenchymal CT), highly vascular, innermost meninx.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The inner surface of dura mater is lined by.
questions.explanation: The inner surface of dura mater (which faces the arachnoid) is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium). The outer surface is attached to periosteum. This creates the dural sinus spaces between the two layers.
