questions.keyConcept: Dura mater: outer surface = periosteum; inner surface = simple squamous mesothelium facing arachnoid.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The brain CSF barrier is not formed of:
questions.explanation: The brain-CSF barrier is formed by ependymal cells connected by tight junctions, basement membrane, and astrocyte foot processes. Fenestrated endothelial cells are NOT part of this barrier - the brain capillary endothelium has tight junctions forming the blood-brain barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Brain-CSF barrier: ependymal tight junctions + basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes.
options: Ependymal cells connected by tight junction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The blood CSF barrier is not formed of:
questions.explanation: Foot processes of astrocytes are part of the BLOOD-BRAIN barrier, not the blood-CSF barrier. The blood-CSF barrier consists of fenestrated capillaries, basement membrane, and choroid plexus epithelium (connected by tight junctions).
questions.keyConcept: Blood-CSF barrier: fenestrated capillaries + choroid epithelium with tight junctions. Blood-brain barrier: tight junction endothelium + astrocyte foot processes.
options: Endothelial cells of fenestrated blood capillaries
Ependymal cells connected by tight junction.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: tight junction between ependymal cells forms:
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form the brain-CSF barrier, limiting passage between ventricles and brain parenchyma. The blood-brain barrier involves astrocyte foot processes and tight junction endothelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal tight junctions = brain-CSF barrier. Astrocyte foot processes + endothelial tight junctions = blood-brain barrier.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein specific to astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in histology and neuropathology. Oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells do not contain GFAP.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP: astrocyte marker (intermediate filament). Used to identify astrocytes in CNS.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following share in the cerebellar islands:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar islands (islands of granular cells) contain rosettes of mossy fiber terminals surrounded by dendrites of granule cells. Mossy fibers synapse with granule cell dendrites in these glomeruli.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar glomeruli: mossy fiber rosettes + granule cell dendrites; input from spinal cord/brainstem.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cerebellar glomeruli contain the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar glomeruli contain rosettes of mossy fibers, dendrites of granule cells, and axons of Golgi cells (inhibitory). They do NOT contain dendrites of basket cells - those are involved in different synapses on Purkinje cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar glomerulus: mossy fiber rosette + granule cell dendrites + Golgi cell axons. Basket cells synapse on Purkinje soma.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The main efferent fiber of the cerebellar cortex is formed by axons of:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the SOLE OUTPUT of the cerebellar cortex - their axons are the only fibers leaving the cortex to deeper nuclei. These axons are inhibitory (GABAergic). Golgi, basket, and granule cells are all interneurons.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cells: only efferent of cerebellar cortex; GABAergic; projects to deep nuclei and vestibular nuclei.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Cerebellar cortex:
questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex is NOT uniform - different regions have different afferent inputs (vestibular, spinocerebellar, corticocerebellar). It has 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), not 6. It does show sulci (folia).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex: 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), folia/sulci, non-uniform structure.
options: Contain martonitti cells in the molecular layer.
Is of uniform structure all over cerebellum

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Climbing fibers:
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers are the axons of contralateral inferior olivary nucleus neurons. They ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and climb on Purkinje cell dendrites. They carry error signals for motor learning. Mossy fibers (not climbing) end in granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers: olivocerebellar (contralateral ION), climb on Purkinje dendrites, carry error signals.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following tracts carries the climbing fibers of cerebellum?
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers travel via the olivocerebellar tract through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum. The dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the trunk. The pontocerebellar tract carries mossy fibers from the pontine nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Olivocerebellar tract: inferior cerebellar peduncle → climbing fibers to cerebellum.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The molecular layer of cerebellum contains which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The molecular layer of cerebellum contains stellate cells (with cell bodies here), basket cells (with cell bodies here), and the dendrites of Purkinje cells and Golgi cells. Purkinje cell bodies are in the Purkinje layer. Golgi cell bodies are in the granular layer. Cerebellar glomeruli are in the granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar molecular layer: stellate + basket cells, Purkinje/Golgi dendrites. Purkinje layer: Purkinje cell bodies. Granular layer: granule cells, Golgi bodies, glomeruli.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The deepest layer of the cerebellar cortex is
questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex has 3 layers: molecular layer (outer), Purkinje cell layer (middle), and granular layer (deepest/innermost). The granular layer contains granule cells, Golgi cells, and cerebellar glomeruli.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex layers (superficial to deep): molecular → Purkinje → granular.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the following statements are correctly describing the pyramidal cells except:
questions.explanation: In pyramidal cells, the APEX (where the thick branching dendrite arises) is directed INWARD toward the white matter, and the BASE is directed toward the cortical surface. The axon emerges from the base. Betz cells are indeed giant pyramidal cells in the motor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal cell orientation: apex (dendrite) faces inward (white matter); base (axon) faces outward (surface).
options: The apex is directed to the cortical surface, a thick branching dendrite arises from the base of the cell and passes into the underlying white matter.
They are well developed in motor centers.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the following are histological layers of the cerebral cortex except:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are characteristic of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex has 6 layers: molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal, and multiform. The cerebellar cortex has 3 layers.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex layers: I-VI (6 layers). Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular (3 layers).

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: All of the following are cells of the cerebral cortex except:
questions.explanation: All of these - pyramidal cells, granular cells, fusiform cells, and Martinotti cells - ARE cells of the cerebral cortex. Pyramidal cells are the most common excitatory neurons. Granular cells are small interneurons. Fusiform cells are in the deep layer. Martinotti cells have ascending axons.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex neurons: pyramidal (main), granular, fusiform, Martinotti, basket, Chandelier cells.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The outer band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL GRANULAR layer (layer IV). This band represents dense termination of thalamocortical fibers. The inner band of Baillarger is in the internal pyramidal layer (layer V).
questions.keyConcept: Outer Baillarger: layer IV (internal granular) - thalamocortical input. Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal).

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The inner band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The inner band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V), which contains Betz cells in the motor cortex and other pyramidal neurons. The horizontal myelinated fibers form this band.
questions.keyConcept: Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal) - contains Betz cells and corticospinal neurons.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The cytoplasm of astrocytes contains
questions.explanation: Astrocytes contain microtubules (for transport), GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein - their intermediate filament marker), and thread-like mitochondria. These contents help identify astrocytes histologically. GFAP is the most specific marker.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte cytoplasm: GFAP (marker), microtubules, mitochondria. GFAP used for astrocyte identification.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about microglia?
questions.explanation: Microglia are present in CNS including retina and optic nerve (CNS outgrowths). They are small spindle-shaped cells with branching poles and fine spines on their surfaces. They are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages, spindle-shaped with branched spiny processes, mesodermal origin.
options: They are present in the retina and optic nerve
They are small spindle shaped cells with branching poles
The cell body and processes have minute spines on their surfaces

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fibers of vagus nerve exit ….
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) exits the brainstem between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle, at the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla. This is the same level where glossopharyngeal and accessary nerves also emerge.
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nerve: exits between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle at posterolateral sulcus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nuclei receive the GSA fibers of facial nerve:
questions.explanation: GSA (general somatic afferent) fibers of the facial nerve carry proprioception from facial muscles and sensation from a small area of the external ear. These fibers relay in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, which spans the pons and medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve GSA: relays in spinal nucleus of trigeminal (same as other facial sensation).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cranial nerve whose component is Only GSE:
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) has ONLY general somatic efferent (GSE) fibers, supplying the extrinsic and intrinsic muscles of the tongue. Other cranial nerves have mixed components. The vagus, glossopharyngeal, and accessory nerves all have visceral components.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII (hypoglossal): only GSE fibers to tongue muscles. Vagus: GSE + GVE + SVA + GVA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Spinal n. of trigeminal, equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is equivalent to substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II) of the spinal cord dorsal horn. Both are involved in pain and temperature transmission. The main sensory nucleus handles fine touch; Clarke's nucleus is for proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of V = substantia gelatinosa (pain/temp). Main sensory nucleus = epicritic touch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nuclei of the vagus nerve include the following except:
questions.explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the vagus. The vagus has: nucleus ambiguus (branchial GSE), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (GVE), and solitary nucleus (SVA, GVA).
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (motor), dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic), solitary nucleus (sensory).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cranial nerve nucleus in floor of 4th ventricle close to midline in lower pons is:
questions.explanation: The abducent nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, close to the midline in the lower pons. It supplies the lateral rectus muscle. The facial motor nucleus is more lateral, and the hypoglossal nucleus is in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Abducent nucleus: floor of 4th ventricle, lower pons, near midline; supplies lateral rectus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The only cranial nerve that decussate before its emergence is:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the ONLY cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) before emerging from the brainstem. It decussates in the superior medullary velum. All other cranial nerves emerge without crossing.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV (trochlear): only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence; crosses in superior medullary velum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are present in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (crossing fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei) are present in the CLOSED MEDULLA where they sweep around the central gray to form the medial lemniscus. In the open medulla, these fibers have already crossed and ascended.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers: cross in closed medulla, sweep around central gray to form medial lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT
questions.explanation: The main inferior olivary nucleus is present in the OPEN (not closed) medulla, located ventrolaterally. The closed medulla contains: motor decussation (lower), sensory decussation (higher), gracile and cuneate nuclei and tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla: decussations, gracile/cuneate nuclei. Open medulla: inferior olivary nucleus.
options: in the lower part there are motor decussation
at a higher level there are sensory decussation
contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cranial nerves in medulla oblongata are the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) emerges from the PONS (at pontomedullary junction), not the medulla. The medullary cranial nerves are: IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal).
questions.keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: CN IX, X, XI, XII. CN VII (facial) is pontine.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Gracile & Cuneate N. are present in:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the DORSAL aspect of the closed medulla, forming the tubercles seen on the posterior surface. These nuclei receive proprioception and fine touch from the lower and upper body respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei: dorsal closed medulla; receive proprioception and fine touch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Crossing fibers of gracile & cuneate tracts are called:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are the DECUSSATING (crossing) fibers of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal system. They cross in the sensory decussation of the closed medulla and form the medial lemniscus. External arcuate fibers are cerebellar afferents.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers: cross in sensory decussation → form medial lemniscus. External arcuate: cerebellar afferents.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lowermost level of medulla shows:
questions.explanation: The lowermost medulla (near spinomedullary junction) shows the DECUSSATION OF CORTICOSPINAL FIBERS (motor decussation). The pyramids are not yet formed. The inferior olivary nucleus appears at higher (open medulla) levels. Superior olive is pontine.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal decussation: lowermost medulla (motor decussation). Sensory decussation is higher. Olivary nucleus is higher still.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Arcuate nucleus is found in:
questions.explanation: The arcuate nucleus is found VENTRAL to the pyramids, in the anterior median fissure. It is a relay nucleus in the corticocerebellar pathway. It receives input from the cortex and projects to the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Arcuate nucleus: ventral to pyramids, in anterior median fissure; pontocerebellar relay.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from:
questions.explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the ARCUATE NUCLEUS (not the cuneate nucleus which projects to cerebellum via dorsal external arcuate fibers). The arcuate nucleus receives corticofugal fibers and projects to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate: from arcuate nucleus → cerebellum (via ICP). Dorsal external arcuate: from accessory cuneate → cerebellum.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Accessory cuneate nucleus give rise to:
questions.explanation: The accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus gives rise to UNCROSSED fibers that ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum (cuneocerebellar tract). These carry proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus: uncrossed fibers → cerebellum via ICP; proprioception from upper limb.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The central gray in upper closed medulla contains:
questions.explanation: The central gray (around the central canal) in the upper closed medulla contains the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. At this level, it is continuous with the spinal nucleus in the medulla. The nucleus solitarius is more lateral.
questions.keyConcept: Central gray upper medulla: spinal nucleus of V. More laterally: nucleus solitarius. Ventrally: inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in the UPPER level of closed medulla where the sensory decussation occurs. At the lower level, the motor decussation is occurring. In the open medulla, the medial lemniscus has already formed and ascended.
questions.keyConcept: Upper closed medulla: sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers). Lower closed medulla: motor decussation.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system due to its connections with:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation controls the endocrine system through its extensive connections with the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is the main link between the nervous system and the endocrine system, and the reticular formation modulates hypothalamic function.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation → hypothalamus → pituitary → endocrine control. RF also influences autonomic functions via hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Inferior olivary nucleus:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers). It is located in the OPEN medulla, not ventral aspect. Its efferent fibers decussate and reach the CONTRALATERAL cerebellar cortex through the INFERIOR cerebellar peduncle as climbing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary: receives rubral input, in open medulla, projects via ICP to contralateral cerebellum as climbing fibers.
options: Present in the ventral aspect of closed medulla.
Its efferent fibers reach the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
Its efferent fibers are the mousy fibers reaching the cerebellar cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: One of the relays nuclel of auditory pathway is:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus. The trapezoid body also passes through this area.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive (binaural hearing) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sections In lower level of pons show.
questions.explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the MIDDLE cerebellar peduncle (the largest cerebellar peduncle, connecting pons to cerebellum). The superior cerebellar peduncle is more superior. The mesencephalic nucleus of V is in the midbrain. Medial and inferior vestibular nuclei are in the upper medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle. Midbrain: superior cerebellar peduncle. Medulla: inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Basis pontis contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Basis pontis contains corticospinal fibers (descending to spinal cord), corticonuclear fibers (to cranial nerve nuclei), and transverse pontine fibers (to cerebellum). Pontine reticulospinal fibers are in the tegmentum (not basis), along with other tegmental structures.
questions.keyConcept: Basis pontis: corticospinal, corticonuclear, transverse pontine fibers. Tegmentum: reticulospinal, sensory nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Auditory pathways contain the following except:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus carries somatosensory information (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), not auditory information. Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB → auditory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: About substantia nigra, all true except:
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is present DORSAL to the cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri), not ventral. It consists of pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons) and pars reticularis. It is connected to the basal ganglia circuit. Its dopamine content gives it its dark color.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra: dorsal to crus cerebri, contains dopamine, connected to basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT.
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus has 4 layers (stratum zonale, stratum cinereum, stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci), not 5. The stratum basilare (basal layer) is not a recognized layer of the superior colliculus. It is part of the visual reflex pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers (superficial to deep): zonale → cinereum → opticum → lemnisci. Not stratum basilare.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The tract in MLB responsible for head righting reflex is:
questions.explanation: The interstitiospinal tract (from interstitial nucleus of Cajal) is primarily responsible for the head righting reflex, which maintains head position in space. The tectospinal tract is for neck reflexes in response to visual stimuli. Vestibulospinal maintains posture. Reticulospinal for autonomic functions.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitiospinal tract: from interstitial nucleus of Cajal, head righting reflex, descends in MLF.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The specific feature of upper mid brain is presence of:
questions.explanation: The SUPERIOR cerebellar peduncle DECUSSATION is specific to the upper midbrain - it carries cerebellar output to the thalamus. The crus cerebri and substantia nigra are present throughout the midbrain. Red nucleus is present in the upper midbrain but its decussation is not unique to upper level.
questions.keyConcept: Upper midbrain specific feature: decussation of superior cerebellar peduncles (dentatothalamic fibers).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Central tegmental tract contains fibers connect between:
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract connects the red nucleus (midbrain) to the inferior olivary nucleus (medulla). It carries rubroreticular and reticuloolivary fibers. This pathway is important for motor learning and coordination.
questions.keyConcept: Central tegmental tract: red nucleus ↔ inferior olivary nucleus (olivocerebellar pathway).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial longitudinal bundle, all true except:
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) extends from the brainstem to the CERVICAL spinal cord, not the whole length. It connects vestibular nuclei to the spinal cord for head and neck movement coordination. It does not extend into the lumbosacral cord.
questions.keyConcept: MLF: brainstem to cervical cord; connects vestibular nuclei to control head/neck movements.
options: receive ascending & descending fibers from vestibular nuclei.
Function for movement of the head & neck
extending from brainstem till cervical segments of spinal cord.
Extend the whole length of spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Dorsal tegmental decussation:
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the TECTOSPINAL tract, which crosses at the level of the inferior colliculus in the midbrain. It descends to control neck muscles in response to visual stimuli. It is not the rubrospinal tract and does not descend in all spinal segments.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation: tectospinal tract crosses at inferior colliculus level, controls neck muscles.
options: Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.
Present in inferior level of midbrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Superior cerebellar decussation:
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar decussation is present at the level of the INFERIOR colliculus (lower midbrain), where dentatothalamic fibers cross. The tectospinal tract forms the dorsal tegmental decussation. Superior cerebellar peduncle fibers pass through the midbrain, not ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar decussation: at inferior colliculus level, dentatothalamic fibers cross.
options: Present in inferior level of midbrain.
Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Superior colliculus, all true except:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus is NOT directly connected to the occipital cortex - that connection is via the visual cortex and lateral geniculate body. The superior colliculus is connected to the retina (via retinal ganglion cells), and gives rise to the tectospinal tract and dorsal tegmental decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus: connected to retina, not occipital cortex; gives tectospinal and dorsal tegmental decussation.
options: Give tectospinal tract & dorsal tegmental decussation.
Present in tectum of the upper midbrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nuclei extend in the midbrain:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve extends through the midbrain (alongside the central gray). It is the only sensory nucleus that contains primary afferent cell bodies. Vestibular nuclei are in the pons/medulla. Motor facial is pontine. Superior olive is pontine.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus of V: only primary afferent neuron in CNS, extends through midbrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fibers derived from which nucleus run transversally to form the trapezoid body?
questions.explanation: The VENTRAL cochlear nucleus gives rise to fibers that cross transversely to form the trapezoid body in the pons. These are part of the auditory pathway to the superior olivary nucleus. The dorsal cochlear nucleus projects via the intermediate acoustic stria.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral cochlear nucleus → trapezoid body → superior olivary nucleus (auditory pathway).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following tracts are present in the tegmentum pontis?
questions.explanation: The tegmentum pontis (pontine tegmentum) contains all of these: medial longitudinal fasciculus (vestibulo-ocular), spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature), and central tegmental tract (red nucleus to inferior olive).
questions.keyConcept: Pontine tegmentum: MLF, spinothalamic, central tegmental tracts. Basis pontis: corticospinal, transverse pontine fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the lateral lemniscus formed of?
questions.explanation: The lateral lemniscus is formed from ALL THREE acoustic stria (dorsal, intermediate, and ventral) plus fibers from the superior olivary nucleus and trapezoid body nuclei. It carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei to the inferior colliculus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral lemniscus: from all 3 acoustic stria + superior olive + trapezoid nuclei → inferior colliculus.
options: Fibers from the nuclei of the trapezoid body

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the TECTOSPINAL tract. Fibers from the superior colliculus cross in the dorsal tegmentum at the inferior colliculus level to descend and control neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation: tectospinal tract crosses at inferior colliculus level.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The ventral tegmental decussation is formed by
questions.explanation: The VENTRAL tegmental decussation is formed by the RUBROSPINAL tract. Fibers from the red nucleus cross in the midbrain (at superior colliculus level) to descend and control limb flexor muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral tegmental decussation: rubrospinal tract crosses at superior colliculus level.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Six hours after a meal, which of the following is (are) MOST important as a source of fuel for the brain?
questions.explanation: After 6 hours post-meal (fasting state), the brain relies primarily on ketone bodies (from hepatic fatty acid oxidation) as its main fuel. Glycogen stores are depleted. Fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently. Protein is not a primary brain fuel.
questions.keyConcept: Brain fuel: glucose (fed) → ketone bodies (fasting). Ketone bodies cross BBB and replace glucose after prolonged fasting.
options: Fatty acids from the adipose tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (serotonin-secreting tumor) is diagnosed by measuring 5-Hydroxyindole-acetic acid (5-HIAA) in 24-hour urine - this is the main serotonin metabolite. 5-HIAA is elevated in carcinoid tumors. VMA is for pheochromocytoma. Phenylacetylglutamine is a phenylalanine metabolite.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid diagnosis: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite). VMA = catecholamine metabolite (pheochromocytoma).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may serve as a tumor marker?
questions.explanation: Both VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) and 5-HIAA can serve as tumor markers - VMA for neuroblastoma/pheochromocytoma, and 5-HIAA for carcinoid tumors. Phenylpyruvic acid is not a tumor marker.
questions.keyConcept: Tumor markers: VMA (neuroblastoma/pheochromocytoma), 5-HIAA (carcinoid). Both can be measured.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is Important for synthesis of both epinephrine and melatonin?
questions.explanation: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AAAD) converts 5-HTP to serotonin (for melatonin synthesis) and DOPA to dopamine (for epinephrine synthesis). This enzyme is required for both pathways, making it the shared enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: AAAD: converts 5-HTP→serotonin (→melatonin) and DOPA→dopamine (→norepinephrine→epinephrine).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Catecholamines
questions.explanation: Catecholamines include dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. They function both as neurotransmitters (in the CNS and autonomic nervous system) and as hormones (epinephrine from adrenal medulla). Both statements (a) and (b) are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines (dopamine, NE, E): both neurotransmitters and hormones. Synthesized from tyrosine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All of the following are ketogenic Amino acids except:
questions.explanation: Glycine is a glucogenic amino acid, not ketogenic. Leucine and isoleucine are purely ketogenic. Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic. Lysine is also purely ketogenic. Glycine is converted to serine (glucogenic) or to porphyrins.
questions.keyConcept: Purely ketogenic: leucine, lysine. Both glucogenic/ketogenic: isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan. Glucogenic: glycine, alanine, serine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The main sites for oxidative deamination are:
questions.explanation: Oxidative deamination (conversion of amino acids to keto acids with release of ammonia) occurs mainly in the LIVER and KIDNEY. These organs have the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase. Other tissues lack significant oxidative deamination capacity.
questions.keyConcept: Oxidative deamination: liver and kidney (glutamate dehydrogenase). Produces ammonia for urea cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The urea cycle is active in cases of
questions.explanation: The urea cycle is active during protein intake (to excrete excess nitrogen) and during fasting (when protein breakdown increases to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis). Both conditions increase nitrogen waste that must be excreted as urea.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle: active during high protein intake and fasting (increased amino acid catabolism).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The major end product of protein nitrogen metabolism in man is:
questions.explanation: Urea is the major end product of protein nitrogen metabolism in humans, produced exclusively in the liver via the urea cycle. It is excreted by the kidneys. Ammonia is toxic and must be converted to urea. Uric acid is from purine metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Major nitrogen waste product: urea (from hepatic urea cycle). Ammonia is converted to urea.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: If there were complete absence of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, what would be the source of urea in the blood?
questions.explanation: With CPS-I deficiency, urea cannot be synthesized via the cycle. However, some urea is produced by bacterial action on ammonia in the gut (bacterial urease). The liver's arginase cannot produce urea without upstream cycle intermediates.
questions.keyConcept: CPS-I deficiency: some urea from bacterial urease in intestine, not from hepatic urea cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: N-acetyl glutamate is an essential allosteric activator of:
questions.explanation: N-acetyl glutamate (NAG) is an essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I), the first enzyme of the urea cycle in mitochondria. NAG is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase.
questions.keyConcept: N-acetylglutamate: allosteric activator of CPS-I (first urea cycle enzyme). Synthesized from acetyl-CoA + glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following increases with deficiency of any enzyme of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: When any urea cycle enzyme is deficient, ammonia cannot be efficiently converted to urea. Glutamine synthesis (via glutamine synthetase) increases as an alternative ammonia detoxification pathway, so glutamine levels increase.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle deficiency: increased glutamine (alternative ammonia detoxification). Citrulline may decrease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following may be true about the glutamine synthetase reaction in the brain?
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase in astrocytes converts glutamate + ammonia → glutamine. This normally detoxifies ammonia. At high ammonia, glutamate gets depleted, reducing GABA synthesis (since GABA is made from glutamate), causing neurological symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glutamine synthetase: detoxifies ammonia; depletes glutamate → reduced GABA → neurological dysfunction.
options: At high ammonia concentration, it can deplete glutamate, with consequent decrease of GABA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of GLUTAMINE (via glutamine synthetase in astrocytes). The brain uses this pathway to detoxify ammonia. Alanine synthesis occurs in liver (not brain). Glutamate is made from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia but requires different enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Normal ammonia disposal in brain: glutamine synthetase (astrocytes) converts glutamate + NH3 → glutamine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia toxicity to the brain is Probably through which of the Following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Ammonia toxicity primarily inhibits the citric acid cycle (energy production) by depleting alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamate. It does NOT increase GABA (it decreases it). It causes alkalosis (not acidosis). Brain can still use amino acids.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibits TCA cycle (depletes alpha-ketoglutarate), depletes glutamate → decreased GABA → neurological symptoms.
options: Inhibition of energy production in brain Cells.
Production of increased amounts of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
Acidifying effect on the intra- and extracellular fluids.
Conversion to urea, increasing the Osmotic pressure.
Inability of the brain cells to utilize any of the amino acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hyperammonemia may be caused by
questions.explanation: Primary hyperammonemia results from genetic defects in any urea cycle enzyme. Secondary hyperammonemia results from liver failure (inability to convert ammonia to urea). Both causes lead to ammonia accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonemia: primary (urea cycle enzyme defect) or secondary (liver failure). Both cause ammonia accumulation.
options: genetic defect of any enzyme of urea cycle (primary hyperammonemia).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The symptom of ammonia intoxication includes.
questions.explanation: Ammonia intoxication primarily affects the brain, causing mental confusion, asterixis (liver flap), and eventually coma. It does not typically cause visual blurring, constipation, or diarrhea as primary symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia intoxication: brain dysfunction → mental confusion, asterixis, coma. Does not cause GI symptoms primarily.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia Levels are.
questions.explanation: Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia levels are INCREASED (elevated). Normal brain ammonia is kept very low by glutamine synthesis and urea cycle. Elevated ammonia causes the neurological symptoms described.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia intoxication: occurs when brain ammonia levels are elevated, disrupting glutamate/GABA metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Primary hyperammonemia may be treated by
questions.explanation: Primary hyperammonemia (urea cycle defects) is treated with: low-protein diet (reduce nitrogen load), benzoic acid/phenylacetate (alternative nitrogen excretion as conjugated amino acids), and acidification of intestinal lumen (to trap ammonia as NH4+ for excretion).
questions.keyConcept: Primary hyperammonemia treatment: low protein, alternative nitrogen excretion (benzoic acid, phenylacetate), gut ammonia trapping.
options: agents that increase excretion of Conjugated amino acids, e.g., benzoic acid and phenylacetate.
acidification of the intestinal lumen to help get rid of ammonia as ammonium Ions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Maple syrup urine disease is an inborn error of metabolism of:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease involves defective metabolism of BRANCHED CHAIN AMINO ACIDS (leucine, isoleucine, valine) due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Accumulated metabolites give urine a maple syrup odor.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease: branched-chain amino acid metabolism defect (BCKDH deficiency).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Phenylketonuria is caused by deficiency of
questions.explanation: PKU results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This deficiency prevents the normal metabolism of phenylalanine, leading to accumulation and conversion to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate).
questions.keyConcept: PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → converted to phenylketones → intellectual disability if untreated.
options: Conversion of phenylalanine to  a phenylketoacid.
Production of phenylalanine from  a phenylketoacid.
Reaction of phenylalanine with an α-ketoacid.
Conversion of phenylalanine to another aminoacid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Conversion of Phenylalanine to tyrosine is catalyzed by phenylalanine hydroxylase which requires.
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, along with oxygen and NADPH. BH4 is also required for tyrosine hydroxylase (dopamine synthesis) and tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin synthesis).
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase: requires BH4, O2, NADPH. BH4 deficiency causes malignant PKU.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The major contributor to the one-carbon pool?
questions.explanation: Serine is the major contributor to the one-carbon pool through its conversion to glycine, releasing a methylene group (-CH2-). The methyl group can be transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming N5,N10-methylene-THF.
questions.keyConcept: One-carbon pool: serine → glycine transfers CH2 to THF. Also from histidine, tryptophan, methionine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Methionine is synthesized in human body from:
questions.explanation: Methionine is synthesized from homocysteine and serine via methionine synthase (requires B12) and other enzymes. The pathway involves converting homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate.
questions.keyConcept: Methionine synthesis: homocysteine + serine → methionine (requires B12, folate). Cysteine is made from serine + homocysteine separately.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hyper-homocysteinemia may result from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of pyridoxine (B6, needed for transsulfuration to cysteine), cobalamin (B12, needed for remethylation to methionine), or folic acid (needed for the folate cycle that donates methyl groups).
questions.keyConcept: Hyperhomocysteinemia: B6, B12, or folate deficiency → elevated homocysteine → cardiovascular risk, neurological issues.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Muscle of facial expression are developed from which pharyngeal arch: ___
questions.explanation: Muscles of facial expression are derived from the second pharyngeal arch (stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, stapedius, and all muscles of facial expression). The second arch is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.keyConcept: Second pharyngeal arch: muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric. Nerve: CN VII (facial).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of first somatosensory area cause?
questions.explanation: The first somatosensory area receives sensory input from the contralateral body. A lesion causes contralateral hemianesthesia (loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body). The face area is in the lower part, upper limb in middle, and lower limb on the medial surface.
questions.keyConcept: First somatosensory area: postcentral gyrus; lesion → contralateral hemianesthesia (loss of all sensation).
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemianesthesia (loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body). More detailed: loss of fine touch, proprioception, and stereognosis on the contralateral side, particularly affecting the distal parts of limbs more than proximal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of first somatosensory area?
questions.explanation: The first somatosensory area (S1) is located in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and extends onto the posterior part of the paracentral lobule (representing the lower limb). The face is represented in the lower part near the lateral sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: First somatosensory area: postcentral gyrus + posterior paracentral lobule (leg representation).
questions.modelAnswer: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and posterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). The body representation is inverted: face near Sylvian fissure, upper limb in middle, trunk higher up, lower limb on medial surface (paracentral lobule).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of second somatosensory area?
questions.explanation: The second somatosensory area (S2) is located in the superior lip of the postcentral gyrus, behind the central sulcus, and extends into the parietal operculum. It receives input from S1 and is involved in more complex sensory processing.
questions.keyConcept: Second somatosensory area: superior lip of postcentral gyrus, parietal operculum, near lateral sulcus.
questions.modelAnswer: Superior lip of post-ramus of lateral sulcus behind the central sulcus. It lies in the parietal operculum and extends into the anterior part of insula. Smaller body representation than S1, bilateral representation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of area 43?
questions.explanation: Area 43 (primary gustatory area) is located in the parietal operculum extending into the anterior part of the insula. It receives taste inputs from the nucleus of the solitary tract via the VPM nucleus of the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Area 43: primary gustatory cortex in parietal operculum and anterior insula.
questions.modelAnswer: Parietal operculum extending into the anterior part of insula. This is the primary gustatory area, receiving taste sensation via the thalamus (VPM).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of Areas 5 & 7 cause?
questions.explanation: Areas 5 and 7 are somatosensory association areas. Lesions cause astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and inability to judge size, shape, and texture of objects despite intact primary sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 5 & 7: somatosensory association cortex; lesion → astereognosis (tactile agnosia).
questions.modelAnswer: Astereognosis - inability to identify objects by touch despite intact primary sensation. The patient cannot recognize the size, shape, or texture of objects placed in their hand.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of inferior parietal lobule?
questions.explanation: The inferior parietal lobule consists of the supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus) and the angular gyrus (around the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule: supramarginal gyrus + angular gyrus. Part of Wernicke's area for language.
questions.modelAnswer: Supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of lateral sulcus) and angular gyrus (around the posterior end of superior temporal sulcus).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of inferior parietal lobule cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule (dominant hemisphere) causes receptive (sensory) aphasia - difficulty understanding language. In the non-dominant hemisphere, it causes contralateral hemisensory neglect.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule lesion: dominant hemisphere → receptive aphasia (Wernicke's area connections).
questions.modelAnswer: Receptive aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia) - fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. Patient speaks fluently but cannot understand or produce meaningful language.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 speech centers?
questions.explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech, inferior frontal gyrus), Wernicke's area (sensory speech, posterior superior temporal gyrus), and the supplementary motor area (medial frontal gyrus).
questions.keyConcept: Speech centers: Broca's (expressive), Wernicke's (receptive), supplementary motor area (planning).
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Broca's area - pars triangularis and opercularis of inferior frontal gyrus (expressive speech). 2) Wernicke's area - posterior superior temporal gyrus (receptive speech). 3) Supplementary motor area - medial frontal gyrus (speech planning and initiation).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of primary motor area?
questions.explanation: The primary motor area (area 4) is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe and extends onto the anterior part of the paracentral lobule on the medial surface (representing the lower limb).
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor area: precentral gyrus + anterior paracentral lobule (leg). Body representation is inverted.
questions.modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus of frontal lobe and anterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). Representation is upside-down and contralateral: face near lateral sulcus, upper limb above, trunk, lower limb on medial surface.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the body representation of premotor area?
questions.explanation: The premotor area has body representation that is upside down and contralateral, similar to the primary motor area. However, the representation is disproportionate - areas requiring skilled movements (hands, face, tongue) have larger representations.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area body map: inverted, contralateral, disproportionate (larger for skilled movements).
questions.modelAnswer: Upside down, contralateral, and the representation is proportionate to skill - larger areas for hands, face, and tongue (requiring fine skilled movements) and smaller areas for trunk and proximal limbs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of Area 4 cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of Area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes contralateral hemiplegia, most affecting fine skilled movements of the distal limbs. The face and hand representations are most affected due to their large cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Area 4 lesion: contralateral hemiplegia, especially fine movements (face, hand). UMN signs below lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia especially affecting fine skilled movements. The paralysis is most pronounced in the distal parts of the contralateral limbs (especially hand and foot), with spasticity and hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron signs).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of premotor area?
questions.explanation: The premotor area (area 6) is located in front of area 4, extending across the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri and onto the medial surface of the hemisphere. It programs movements without direct cortical input to motor neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area: in front of area 4, superior/middle/inferior frontal gyri and medial surface.
questions.modelAnswer: In front of area 4, in the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri, and on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere. It lies anterior to the precentral gyrus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of area 6 cause?
questions.explanation: Area 6 lesion causes apraxia (inability to perform learned movements on command), muscle spasticity (due to release of area 4 from premotor facilitation), and reappearance of primitive grasp reflex. Motor learning is impaired.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 lesion: apraxia, spasticity (UMN release signs), reappearance of primitive reflexes.
questions.modelAnswer: Apraxia (inability to perform coordinated voluntary movements despite intact motor and sensory systems), spasticity of muscles (due to loss of premotor area inhibition on area 4), and reappearance of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of frontal eye field?
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) is located in front of area 6, in the middle frontal gyrus and superior frontal gyrus. It controls conjugate eye movements to the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal eye field: area 8, in superior and middle frontal gyri (in front of premotor area).
questions.modelAnswer: In the superior and middle frontal gyri, in front of the premotor area (area 6). Controls voluntary conjugate eye movements to the opposite side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of Area 8 cause?
questions.explanation: Area 8 lesion causes ipsilateral deviation of both eyes (inability to look to the opposite side). The eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion because the intact hemisphere drives gaze toward itself.
questions.keyConcept: Area 8 lesion: eyes deviate toward the lesion (ipsilateral), cannot look to opposite side.
questions.modelAnswer: Ipsilateral deviation of both eyes (eyes turn toward the side of the lesion) and inability to turn the eyes to the opposite side. Patient cannot voluntarily look to the opposite side of the lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of Broca’s area?
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the pars triangularis and pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. It is the motor speech center, responsible for speech production.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area: inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis + opercularis), dominant hemisphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Pars triangularis and pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere (usually left). This is the motor speech area responsible for expressive language production.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of Areas 44 and 45 cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of areas 44 and 45 (Broca's area) causes expressive (motor) aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension. The patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate words properly.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 44-45 (Broca's) lesion: expressive aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech, good comprehension.
questions.modelAnswer: Expressive (motor) aphasia - the patient has difficulty producing speech, speaks in short, effortful phrases, telegraphic speech. Comprehension is preserved. Patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate properly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the site of supplementary motor area?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (MII, area 6 on the medial surface) is located in the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the paracentral lobule. It is involved in speech planning and initiation.
questions.keyConcept: Supplementary motor area: medial frontal gyrus, medial surface of frontal lobe.
questions.modelAnswer: Medial frontal gyrus (medial surface of frontal lobe), anterior to the paracentral lobule. Also called MII or SMA, involved in planning and initiating complex movements including speech.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of MII cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of the supplementary motor area (MII) causes akinetic mutism - a state of decreased initiative and motivation to move or speak. The patient is awake but cannot initiate voluntary movements or speech.
questions.keyConcept: MII lesion: akinetic mutism - awake but no initiative to move or speak.
questions.modelAnswer: Akinetic mutism - a state of decreased motivation and initiative where the patient is awake and alert but shows no desire to move or speak. Speech is sparse, movements are minimal, despite intact motor pathways.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 neurons that form the pathway of pain and temperature from the body?
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from the body: 1st neuron: dorsal root ganglion → spinal cord dorsal horn. 2nd neuron: substantia gelatinosa/lamina 4 → VPL nucleus of thalamus (decussating as spinothalamic tract). 3rd neuron: VPL → somatosensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Pain/temp pathway (body): DRG → dorsal horn → VPL (decussates at spinal level) → SI cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: First order neuron: cell body in dorsal root ganglion, peripheral process from receptor, central process enters spinal cord. Second order neuron: substantia gelatinosa (lamina 2) for slow pain; nucleus proprius (lamina 4) for fast pain and temperature. Axons cross at spinal level and ascend in spinothalamic tract to VPL nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPL nucleus of thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 neurons that form the pathway of pain and temperature from the face?
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from the face: 1st: trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus of trigeminal. 2nd: spinal nucleus → VPM nucleus of thalamus (via quintothalamic tract). 3rd: VPM → somatosensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Pain/temp pathway (face): trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus of V → VPM → cortex. Crosses in brainstem.
questions.modelAnswer: First order neuron: cell body in trigeminal ganglion, peripheral process from facial skin/mucosa, central process to spinal nucleus of trigeminal. Second order neuron: spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve, axons cross as quintothalamic tract to VPM nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPM nucleus to primary somatosensory cortex (lower face area).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 neurons that form the pathway of crude touch and pressure?
questions.explanation: Crude touch and pressure: 1st: DRG → spinal cord dorsal column. 2nd: nucleus proprius (lamina 4-5) → VPL via anterior spinothalamic tract. 3rd: VPL → somatosensory cortex. This is different from fine touch which travels in dorsal columns.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch/pressure: DRG → nucleus proprius → VPL (via anterior spinothalamic) → cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: First order neuron: dorsal root ganglion cell, central process to dorsal column. Second order neuron: nucleus proprius (laminae 4-5 of dorsal horn), axons cross and ascend in anterior spinothalamic tract to VPL nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPL nucleus of thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the sensations carried by dorsal column tracts?
questions.explanation: The dorsal column tracts (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry epicritic sensations: fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, stereognosis, and two-point discrimination. These are precise, discriminative sensory modalities.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal columns: fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, stereognosis. Epicritic sensations.
questions.modelAnswer: Fine touch, proprioception (conscious), vibration sense, deep pressure, and stereognosis (recognition of size, shape, and texture of objects). These are discriminative tactile and proprioceptive sensations that require intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 neurons that for the pathway of conscious proprioception and fine touch?
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception and fine touch: 1st neuron: DRG → medulla (dorsal columns). 2nd neuron: gracile/cuneate nuclei → VPL via internal arcuate fibers (decussation = sensory decussation). 3rd neuron: VPL → SI cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Conscious proprioception: DRG → gracile/cuneate nuclei → VPL (decussates in medulla) → cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: First order neuron: dorsal root ganglion cell, central process ascends in dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis for lower body, fasciculus cuneatus for upper body) to the medulla. Second order neuron: gracile and cuneate nuclei of medulla, axons cross as internal arcuate fibers (sensory decussation) to form medial lemniscus to VPL nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPL nucleus of thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the four tracts that carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The four tracts carrying unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum are: posterior spinocerebellar (lower limb, from Clarke's column), anterior spinocerebellar (both limbs, from spinal border cells), spino-olivary (to inferior olive then cerebellum), and cuneocerebellar (upper limb, from accessory cuneate nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum: posterior and anterior spinocerebellar, spino-olivary, cuneocerebellar tracts.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column, lower limb). 2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract (from spinal border cells, both limbs). 3) Spino-olivary tract (to inferior olivary nucleus, then to cerebellum). 4) Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper limb).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tract forms the external arcuate fibers?
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract forms the external arcuate fibers. These fibers arise from the accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus and enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract: from accessory cuneate nucleus → external arcuate fibers → cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: The cuneocerebellar tract. Its fibers arise from the accessory cuneate nucleus and form the external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: List the tracts that carry unconscious proprioception from the lower limb.
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb is carried to the cerebellum by: posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus, T1-L2), anterior spinocerebellar tract (from spinal border cells), and spino-olivary tract (to inferior olive then cerebellum).
questions.keyConcept: Lower limb unconscious proprioception: posterior spinocerebellar, anterior spinocerebellar, spino-olivary tracts.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract - from Clarke's column (T1-L2) ascends in spinal cord to enter cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle. 2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract - from spinal border cells, ascends and enters via superior cerebellar peduncle (fibers cross back in cerebellum). 3) Spino-olivary tract - synapses in inferior olivary nucleus, then olivocerebellar fibers enter cerebellum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention 2 extrapyramidal tracts.
questions.explanation: The two major extrapyramidal tracts (motor pathways outside the corticospinal tract) are the tectospinal tract (from superior colliculus, controls neck muscles) and the rubrospinal tract (from red nucleus, controls limb flexor muscles).
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: tectospinal (neck control), rubrospinal (flexor muscles). Both modulate movement.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Tectospinal tract - originates from superior colliculus, crosses in dorsal tegmental decussation, descends to cervical spinal cord to control neck and upper trunk muscles in response to visual stimuli. 2) Rubrospinal tract - originates from red nucleus, crosses in ventral tegmental decussation, descends to control flexor muscles of the upper limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the origin of olivo spinal tract?
questions.explanation: The olivospinal tract originates from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla. It descends to the spinal cord and is involved in motor learning and coordination, carrying error signals from the olive to the cerebellum via climbing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Olivospinal tract: from inferior olivary nucleus. The olive receives input from red nucleus and cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla. The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers) and cerebellar nuclei, and its efferent fibers form the olivospinal tract and olivocerebellar tract (climbing fibers).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which tracts end on alpha and gamma neurons of extensor muscle?
questions.explanation: The vestibulospinal tracts (medial and lateral) end on both alpha and gamma motor neurons of extensor muscles, facilitating antigravity tone and postural stability. The medial vestibulospinal tract descends in the MLF to cervical levels; the lateral vestibulospinal tract descends throughout the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulospinal tracts: medial (MLF, cervical) and lateral (spinal cord) - facilitate extensor muscle tone for posture.
questions.modelAnswer: Medial and lateral vestibulospinal tracts. These tracts facilitate extensor muscle activity to maintain posture and balance against gravity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the lamination of of fibers in the lateral corticospinal tract in the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract shows somatotopic lamination in the spinal cord with cervical fibers located most medially and sacral fibers most laterally. This arrangement reflects the body map with upper extremity representations medial and lower extremity lateral.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal tract lamination: cervical (medial) to sacral (lateral) - inverted somatotopic organization.
questions.modelAnswer: Cervical fibers are medial while sacral fibers are lateral. This medial-to-lateral arrangement from neck to sacrum reflects the body map of the corticospinal tract.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the lamination of pyramidal tract in the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract fibers are organized with fibers for facial muscles in the genu (knee), upper limb fibers most anterior in the posterior limb, and lower limb fibers most posterior in the posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule pyramidal tract: genu = face, anterior posterior limb = upper limb, posterior posterior limb = lower limb.
questions.modelAnswer: Fibers for face muscles are in the genu; upper limb area lies most anterior and lower limb area lies most posterior in the posterior limb of internal capsule. This anterior-to-posterior arrangement in the posterior limb represents head-to-toe body map.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete: Tecto spinal tract forms the dorsal tegmental decussation which the rubro spinal tract forms the ___ tegmental decussation
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract forms the dorsal (posterior) tegmental decussation at the inferior colliculus level. The rubrospinal tract forms the ventral (anterior) tegmental decussation at a slightly higher level. These two decussations separate the neck and limb motor control pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal: dorsal tegmental decussation. Rubrospinal: ventral tegmental decussation. Both control different body regions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 arteries that supply the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord is supplied by three arteries: one anterior spinal artery (running in the anterior median fissure) and two posterior spinal arteries (running near the dorsal roots). Segmental arteries (radicular arteries) reinforce these along the cord length.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord blood supply: anterior spinal artery (1), posterior spinal arteries (2), segmental (radicular) arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery (single, midline), two posterior spinal arteries (lateral), and segmental arteries (multiple, reinforce the longitudinal arteries along the cord length).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery supplies the medial part of medulla oblongata and the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial part of the medulla (including the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus) and the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord (including the anterior and lateral horns and white columns).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: medial medulla + anterior 2/3 spinal cord (all motor and sensory pathways except dorsal columns).
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery. It supplies the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla, and the anterior and lateral horns plus anterior and lateral white columns of the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery supplies the posterior 1/3 of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal arteries (usually two) supply the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, including the dorsal horns and dorsal columns. They run along the posterolateral surfaces near the dorsal nerve roots.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries: posterior 1/3 of spinal cord (dorsal columns and dorsal horns).
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior spinal arteries. They supply the posterior horns and posterior columns of the spinal cord, running along the posterolateral sulcus near the dorsal nerve roots.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the origin of anterior spinal artery?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery is formed by the union of two arteries, each arising from a vertebral artery. The two branches join at the level of the foramen magnum to form a single median anterior spinal artery that descends in the anterior median fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: single median artery formed by union of two branches from vertebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a single median artery formed by the union of two anterior spinal arteries, each being a branch of the corresponding vertebral artery at the level of the medulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the origin of posterior spinal artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior spinal arteries may arise directly from the vertebral artery or from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). They descend as two channels on the posterior surface of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal artery: arises from vertebral artery or PICA.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Either directly from the vertebral artery or as a branch of PICA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the origin of radicular arteries?
questions.explanation: Radicular arteries arise from various sources: vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, posterior intercostal arteries, and the first lumbar artery. They enter the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina and reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, 1st lumbar arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, posterior intercostal arteries, and first lumbar artery. These segmental arteries enter through intervertebral foramina to supply the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 6 veins that drain the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord veins include: one anteromedian vein (in anterior median fissure), one posteromedian vein (on posterior surface), and two each of anterolateral and posterolateral veins running with the nerve roots.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord veins: anteromedian, posteromedian, paired anterolateral and posterolateral veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteromedian vein (in anterior median fissure), posteromedian vein (on posterior surface), and four lateral veins running along the ventral and dorsal nerve roots on each side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the effect of spinal cord complete transverse section?
questions.explanation: Complete transverse section of the spinal cord produces bilateral paralysis below the level of injury. Location determines outcome: above C5 = fatal (respiratory failure); C5-T1 = quadriplegia; below T1 = paraplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord transection: above C5 = death; C5-T1 = quadriplegia; below T1 = paraplegia.
questions.modelAnswer: Above C5: death due to respiratory paralysis. Between C5 and T1: quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs). Below T1: paraplegia (paralysis of lower limbs only).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the effect of spinal cord hemisection?
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection): at lesion level = ipsilateral loss of all sensation + LMNL; below lesion (ipsilateral) = proprioception loss + UMNL; below lesion (contralateral) = pain/temperature loss. This occurs because corticospinal and dorsal columns cross in the brainstem while spinothalamic crosses at spinal level.
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: at level = IPSI all sensation + LMNL; below IPSI = proprioception + UMNL; below CONTRA = pain/temp.
questions.modelAnswer: At the level of lesion (ipsilateral): loss of all types of sensation and lower motor neuron signs. Below the lesion (ipsilateral): loss of proprioception and upper motor neuron signs. Below the lesion (contralateral): loss of pain and temperature sensations. This dissociated sensory loss is characteristic of hemisection.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the effect of anterior spinal artery occlusion?
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes bilateral UMNL paralysis and bilateral loss of pain/temperature below the lesion. Proprioception and fine touch are preserved because the dorsal columns (supplied by posterior spinal arteries) are intact.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: bilateral UMNL + loss pain/temp below, WITH preserved proprioception.
questions.modelAnswer: Bilateral upper motor neuron paralysis below the lesion, bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations below the lesion, with PRESERVATION of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sense (since dorsal columns are intact).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the parts of neostriatum?
questions.explanation: The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen. Together with the globus pallidus, these form the corpus striatum. The caudate and putamen are separated by the internal capsule but are functionally connected.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum: caudate nucleus + putamen. Striatum = neostriatum + paleostriatum (globus pallidus).
questions.modelAnswer: Caudate nucleus and putamen. These are the input nuclei of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical input. They are separated by the internal capsule but functionally linked as the striatum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the parts of paleostriatum?
questions.explanation: The paleostriatum (globus pallidus) consists of two parts: the internal (medial) segment (GPi) and external (lateral) segment (GPe). GPi is the main output nucleus; GPe is part of the indirect pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Paleostriatum: globus pallidus internal (GPi) + external (GPe). GPi = output; GPe = indirect pathway.
questions.modelAnswer: Globus pallidus external (GPe) and globus pallidus internal (GPi). The external segment is part of the indirect pathway; the internal segment is the main output of the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the blood supply of basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus) are supplied by central branches of the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery. The lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) are the primary supply.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia: supplied by lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) and anterior cerebral artery branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Central branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, particularly the lenticulostriate arteries which penetrate the basal ganglia through the anterior perforated substance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the venous drainage of basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia drain into veins that empty into the thalamostriate vein (also called terminal vein), which then drains into the internal cerebral veins and ultimately the great cerebral vein (Galen) into the straight sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia venous drainage: thalamostriate vein → internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein → straight sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Veins that drain into the thalamostriate vein, which courses through the basal ganglia region and empties into the internal cerebral veins, then to the great cerebral vein of Galen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete: The head of caudate bulges into the anterior horn of lateral ventricle, body lies in the floor of body of lateral ventricle, tail lies in the roof of ___ horn of lateral ventricle
questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus follows the lateral ventricle: the head bulges into the anterior horn, the body forms part of the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle, and the tail runs along the roof of the inferior horn before ending in the amygdala.
questions.keyConcept: Caudate nucleus: head = anterior horn floor; body = lateral ventricle floor; tail = inferior horn roof.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the 3 lobes of the cerebellum (Functional classification)?
questions.explanation: The three functional lobes of the cerebellum are: archicerebellum (vestibulocerebellum - flocculonodular lobe), paleocerebellum (spinocerebellum - vermis and paravermis), and neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum - lateral hemispheres).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar functional lobes: archi (vestibular), paleo (spinal), neo (cerebral).
questions.modelAnswer: Archicerebellum (flocculonodular lobe - vestibular connections), paleocerebellum (vermis and paravermis - spinal connections), and neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres - cerebral cortex connections).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the archicerebellum formed of?
